doc_description: American Express Company’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2022, detailing its closed-loop integrated payments model across USCS, CS, ICS and GMNS segments; major partnerships and global merchant/network operations; audited results (revenue $52.9B, net income $7.5B, $1.55T network volumes); capital and regulation (Category IV, CET1 10.3%); and comprehensive risk, governance, and internal control disclosures.

- Securities: Common Shares (par $0.20), trading symbol AXP, listed on the New York Stock Exchange; no securities registered under Section 12(g).

- Filer classification: Large accelerated filer; not an accelerated, non-accelerated, smaller reporting, or emerging growth company.

structure.title: TABLE OF CONTENTS
structure.heading: TABLE OF CONTENTS
structure.summary:
- The document is an Annual Report on Form 10-K for American Express Company, beginning with a comprehensive Table of Contents covering Parts I–IV and an appendix of statistical disclosures for bank holding companies.
- It includes standard SEC sections: Business; Competition; Supervision and Regulation; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market for Common Equity; MD&A (Executive Overview, Consolidated and Segment Results, Capital Resources and Liquidity, Risk Management, Critical Accounting Estimates, Other Matters); Market Risk Disclosures; audited Financial Statements and Notes; Internal Control and Auditor reports; Controls and Procedures; Governance, Compensation, Ownership, Related-Party Transactions, and Auditor Fees; Exhibits; and a Form 10-K Summary and Signatures.
- It contains cautionary forward-looking statements under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, guidance on trademark usage, and definitions of terms used throughout (e.g., “American Express,” “we,” “our”), including a note that “partner” does not imply a legal partnership.
- Item 1 (Business) provides an overview of American Express as a globally integrated payments company and leader in credit and charge cards for consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations, with cards issued by both AmEx and third parties on the American Express network and acceptance by millions of merchants worldwide.
- It describes distribution channels for products and services (mobile/online apps, affiliate marketing, referrals, third-party providers and partners, direct mail, phone, in-house sales, direct response advertising).
- It outlines corporate background and regulatory status: founded in 1850, incorporated in 1965, and operating as a bank holding company under the BHC Act, supervised by the Federal Reserve.
- It identifies four reportable segments—U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS)—with Corporate & Other for remaining activities, and references where segment results appear in MD&A.
- It explains the “integrated payments platform” and “closed-loop” model, emphasizing direct relationships with both Card Members and merchants, access to transaction data at both ends, and how this differentiates AmEx from open bankcard networks.

structure.title: PART I
structure.heading: PART I
structure.start_phrase: American Express is a globally integrated payments company, providing customers with access to products, insights and experiences that enrich lives and build business success.
structure.summary:
- Presents American Express as a globally integrated payments company and leading issuer of credit and charge cards to consumers, small and mid-sized businesses, and large corporations worldwide.
- Notes that cards are issued by both American Express and third-party banks on the American Express network and accepted by millions of merchants globally.
- Describes diverse distribution channels for products and services, including mobile/online applications, affiliate marketing, referrals, third-party providers, business partners, direct mail, telephone, in-house sales, and direct response advertising.
- Provides corporate background and regulatory status: founded in 1850, incorporated in 1965 as a New York corporation; American Express Company and its principal subsidiary TRS are bank holding companies supervised by the Federal Reserve under the BHC Act.
- Outlines reportable operating segments: U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS), with Corporate & Other for corporate functions and certain other businesses.
- Explains the end-to-end integrated payments platform and “closed loop” model, highlighting direct relationships with both Card Members (issuer) and merchants (acquirer), coverage of all key relationship aspects, and differentiation from bankcard networks through direct access to transaction information at both ends.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: 1. Business
structure.start_phrase:
American Express is a globally integrated payments company, providing customers with access to products, insights and experiences that enrich lives and build
business success.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: American Express as a globally integrated payments company and bank holding company under Federal Reserve supervision; core products, channels, and global reach.
- Business structure: Four reportable segments—U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant & Network Services (GMNS)—plus Corporate & Other.
- Integrated “closed-loop” payments platform: Direct relationships with cardmembers and merchants, data advantages for underwriting, fraud prevention, marketing, and offers; inclusion of third-party issuer/acquirer data.
- Card issuing: Broad consumer and commercial card products, rewards, and services; acquisition/retention levers (product design, rewards, digital/mobile, service, partnerships); focus on Millennials/Gen Z and SMEs; adjacent products (business and consumer checking) and acquisitions (Kabbage, Resy, acompay); ICS reorganization and key non-U.S. markets. 2022 metrics: $1,338B billed business; 76.7M proprietary cards-in-force.
- Merchant acquiring (GMNS): Signing and servicing merchants, discount rate setting, relationships with acquirers/aggregators (OptBlue); expanding acceptance, Shop Small campaigns, new payment options (debit, B2B); merchant tools (fraud prevention, marketing, analytics).
- Card network: Partnerships with third-party issuers/acquirers in ~103 countries; licensing the brand and expanding reach. 2022 metrics: $214.5B third-party processed volume; 56.5M third-party cards-in-force.
- Customers and footprint: Diverse base across consumers to large corporates; broad global presence.
- Partnerships: Cobrand and ecosystem relationships (e.g., Delta, Marriott, Hilton, British Airways, Amazon Pay with Points, PayPal, i2c, BILL/BillTrust/Versapay); joint ventures (China, Middle East, Switzerland); GBTG ownership and commercial ties.
- Delta partnership: Largest strategic partner; significant share of volumes (≈10%) and loans (≈21%); extended agreement through 2029; multiple revenue streams and benefits (including lounges).
- Spend-centric model: Revenue emphasis on card spend, annual fees, and high-value customers; value cycle among cardmembers, merchants, and partners.
- Brand and service: Emphasis on trust, security, service excellence; IP protection; awards and customer care focus.
- Strategy: Four imperatives—expand premium consumer leadership, grow/differentiate commercial payments and AP solutions, strengthen global integrated network and merchant value, and leverage global position; digital now embedded. ESG pillars: DE&I, climate solutions, and financial confidence.
- Colleagues and culture: Blue Box Values; ~77,300 employees (2022) with global distribution; talent, benefits, development, wellness; Amex Flex hybrid work; high engagement; diversity metrics and goals; pay equity maintained in 2022.
- Executive leadership: Roles and recent organizational changes for vice chairmen, presidents, and C-suite, including CEO Stephen J. Squeri.
- Competition: Rivalry with global networks (Visa, Mastercard, China UnionPay, etc.), issuers, acquirers, fintechs, digital wallets, buy-now-pay-later, real-time payments, open banking, crypto/blockchain, and other alternatives; key competitive factors (product value, brand, customer spend/credit, acceptance, pricing, innovation, security, and analytics).

structure.title: Competition
structure.heading: Competition
structure.start_phrase:
We compete in the global payments industry with card networks, issuers and acquirers, paper-based transactions (e.g., cash and checks), bank transfer models
(e.g., wire transfers and Automated Clearing House, or ACH), as well as evolving and growing alternative mechanisms, systems and products that leverage new
technologies, business models and customer relationships to create payment, financing or banking solutions.
structure.summary:
- Overview of competitive landscape in the global payments industry, including competition with card networks, issuers, acquirers, cash/checks, bank transfers (ACH/wires), and rapidly growing alternative payment and financing models.
- Company’s competitive positioning as both a card issuer and a global card network; key rivals named (e.g., China UnionPay, Visa, Mastercard, JCB, Discover), with note that the company is the fourth largest network by purchase volume.
- Competitive pressures in premium segments, cobrand partnerships, mobile wallets, private label cards, point-of-sale credit and “buy now, pay later,” and amenities like airport lounges.
- Competition from merchant acquirers, processors, digital and mobile platforms (e.g., Alipay, PayPal, Venmo) and regional networks (e.g., NPCI in India).
- Principal competitive factors: product features and value (rewards, partnerships, travel/lifestyle benefits, digital/mobile), brand, customer base quality and credit performance, merchant acceptance breadth/quality, value to stakeholders (costs, fraud/data capabilities), availability of alternative payments, marketing effectiveness, speed of innovation/tech investment, business expense tools/data, and information security.
- Rapid growth of alternative mechanisms: payment facilitators/aggregators, open banking, e-wallets, POS lenders/BNPL, real-time payments, fintechs, digital currencies (CBDC and private), blockchain, prepaid/gift cards, and account-linked/payments solutions; competitors seeking closed-loop, loyalty and rewards-like advantages.
- Cross-references to Risk Factors on competition, regulatory constraints, and legal proceedings (e.g., non-discrimination and honor-all-cards provisions) that may affect competitiveness.
- Supervision and Regulation overview: extensive global regulatory oversight, high and rising compliance costs, stringent enforcement environment, and ongoing regulatory change affecting practices, pricing, and operations.
- Ongoing regulatory reviews and internal controls leading to changes in products/practices, customer restitution, increased oversight costs, and potential for inquiries, investigations, enforcement actions, and penalties; impact of publicity on regulatory scope.
- Banking regulation specifics: Company and TRS supervised by the Federal Reserve; U.S. bank subsidiary (AENB) supervised by the OCC; CFPB rulemaking, enforcement, and examination authority; regulators’ broad powers (fines, dividend limits, operational/acquisition restrictions, divestitures).
- Activities under the BHC Act and financial holding company status: permissible broader financial activities contingent on being well-capitalized and well-managed and CRA performance; current permissible activities include travel agency services, acting as a finder, and certain insurance services; potential consequences of failing eligibility, including loss of ability to engage in certain activities and make certain acquisitions/investments.

structure.title: Supervision and Regulation
structure.heading: Supervision and Regulation
structure.start_phrase: We are subject to extensive government regulation and supervision in jurisdictions around the world, and the costs of compliance are substantial.
structure.summary:
- Extensive global regulatory and supervisory environment for a large financial services firm, with high compliance costs, evolving risk management, potential product/practice changes, customer restitution, and exposure to inquiries, investigations, enforcement and penalties.
- U.S. banking regulation: consolidated supervision of the parent and key subsidiaries by the Federal Reserve, OCC and CFPB; broad examiner/enforcement authority; additional federal, state and non-U.S. oversight.
- Activities and status: operation as bank and financial holding companies; eligibility requirements to remain a financial holding company (well-capitalized/managed and CRA); consequences of failing eligibility; prohibition of unsafe/unsound practices.
- Acquisitions and investments: prior notice/approval and limitations under federal/state banking laws; significant regulatory discretion over transactions.
- Enhanced prudential standards: tailoring framework places the company (and its bank) in Category IV based on risk indicators; categorization can change over time.
- Capital regulation: Basel III-based Capital Rules; minimum CET1, Tier 1 and Total capital ratios plus SCB for the parent and CCB for the bank; current SCB at 2.5%; leverage ratio requirements; potential for higher capital under Basel 2017 finalization; CECL capital phase-in elected.
- Liquidity standards: heightened liquidity/risk management expectations; LCR and NSFR frameworks exist, but no specific LCR/NSFR requirements for Category IV firms under set thresholds.
- Stress testing and capital planning: CCAR participation; biennial Fed supervisory stress tests for Category IV; annual capital plan submission; SCB recalculated biennially with dividend updates in off years; conditions for plan resubmission and distribution restrictions.
- Dividends and capital distributions: subject to regulatory oversight and buffer constraints; OCC limitations on bank dividends; regulators may restrict payouts deemed unsafe or unsound.
- Prompt corrective action: capital category thresholds and corresponding operational restrictions; brokered deposit constraints if not well capitalized or without FDIC waiver.
- Resolution planning: no holding company plan required for Category IV; insured depository institution (AENB) must submit FDIC resolution plans on a three-year cycle.
- Orderly Liquidation Authority: potential FDIC receivership and SPOE strategy at the holding company level; differences from bankruptcy and implications for creditors.
- FDIC powers at bank insolvency: broad authority to transfer, enforce, or repudiate contracts; priority of U.S. deposit claims over other unsecured claims, including non-U.S. depositors.
- Other banking rules: source-of-strength obligations of the parent to support the bank; affiliate transaction limits; FDIC insurance and assessment framework; CRA obligations and proposed modernization.
- Climate risk supervision: draft principles from OCC, FDIC and Federal Reserve for large institutions on governance, risk management, data, reporting and scenario analysis.
- Consumer financial products: CFPB rulemaking, supervision and enforcement (UDAAP); proposed late fee safe harbor reduction; overlay of state consumer, money transmitter, unclaimed property and insurance laws; heightened international focus on consumer outcomes and responsible lending.
- Payments regulation: global scrutiny of interchange fees, acceptance rules, and network practices; impacts on merchant discount revenue; surcharging/steering trends (including Canada) and associated risks; local licensing/data localization (e.g., India) and operational implications; prior exits from certain network businesses due to regulation.
- Privacy, data protection and cybersecurity: GLBA, CCPA/CPRA, and growing U.S. state requirements; stringent non-U.S. regimes (GDPR/UK GDPR and cross-border transfer frameworks); rising expectations for data governance, resilience and third-party risk management; potential for significant fines and increased costs.
- Financial crimes compliance: AML/CFT obligations under BSA/Patriot Act and AMLA 2020; EU AML directives and other global regimes; heightened reporting and program expectations; sanctions compliance under OFAC, UN, EU; anti-corruption compliance under FCPA and UK Bribery Act with severe penalty risk.
- Compensation oversight: Fed/OCC guidance to align incentives with sound risk management; pending Dodd-Frank incentive compensation rules; SEC 2022 clawback rule for executive compensation following restatements.
- Additional information and other disclosures: investor relations and ESG resources available online; statutory banking disclosures; modest seasonality with higher fourth-quarter volumes and slightly lower discount rate.

structure.title: Additional Information
structure.heading: Additional Information
structure.start_phrase: We maintain an Investor Relations website at http://ir.americanexpress.com.
structure.summary:
- Company information access: Investor Relations website provides free, timely access to SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K and amendments) and routinely posts financial and potentially material updates. ESG and corporate sustainability reports are available on the corporate website.
- Website references: Web content is not incorporated by reference into the report; URLs are provided only as inactive textual references.
- Regulatory disclosure: Certain statistical disclosures required of bank holding companies are provided on page A-1 and incorporated by reference.
- Seasonality: Overall business is not significantly seasonal, but Q4 typically shows moderately higher network volumes, loans and receivables; average discount rate tends to be slightly lower in Q4 due to more retail-related billed business.
- Risk Factors overview (Item 1A): Risks are organized into Strategic/Business/Competitive, Legal/Regulatory/Compliance, and Credit/Liquidity/Market categories, with cross-references to MD&A risk management discussions.
- Macroeconomic sensitivity: Results depend heavily on economic conditions; factors like inflation, interest rates, unemployment, consumer confidence, and policy decisions can affect spending, borrowing, delinquencies, and charge-offs.
- Segment exposure: T&E spending (~25% of 2022 billed business) is highly sensitive to discretionary spending; small business and corporate spending (~45%) depends on the business climate and investment levels.
- Geopolitical and catastrophic events: Geopolitical instability (e.g., Ukraine conflict), policy actions (including U.S. debt ceiling issues), trade tensions, tariffs, labor shortages, government shutdowns, sanctions, terrorism, cyber incidents, natural disasters, severe weather, and health emergencies can adversely affect operations, spending (especially travel), and may trigger travel protection claims.
- COVID-19 impacts: Pandemic caused significant and evolving disruptions; ongoing uncertainties include variants, containment measures, vaccine/treatment effectiveness, inflation, labor and supply-chain issues, the end of support programs, and the pace of normalization—all of which may continue to affect spending, credit performance, and operations.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
This section highlights certain risks that could affect us and our businesses, broadly categorized as “Strategic, Business and Competitive Risks,” “Legal,
Regulatory and Compliance Risks” and “Credit, Liquidity and Market Risks.”
structure.summary:
- The document is a 10-K Table of Contents excerpt focusing on Item 1A Risk Factors, followed by brief Items 1B–4.
- Strategic, business and competitive risks:
  - Macroeconomic sensitivity: revenue and credit performance depend on consumer/business activity; inflation, recession, unemployment, rates, geopolitics (including the Russia-Ukraine conflict), energy prices, policy shifts, and lingering COVID-19 effects can materially affect spending and losses.
  - Revenue mix exposure: travel and entertainment (~25% of 2022 billed business) and small business/corporate spending (~45%) are particularly cyclical.
  - Geopolitical, catastrophic and climate-related events: pandemics, cyber incidents, natural disasters, and severe weather (potentially exacerbated by climate change) can disrupt operations and spending; Russia/Belarus exit increases uncertainty and sanctions/compliance risks.
  - Intense payments competition: pressure from Visa/Mastercard scale, alternative payments (wallets, BNPL, bank transfers), point-of-sale lenders, tech platforms controlling payment choices, and non-traditional players; challenges to merchant acceptance and discount revenue; open banking could erode data advantages.
  - Partner dependence: heavy reliance on cobrand and other partners (e.g., Delta, Marriott, Hilton, British Airways); cobrand portfolios ~18% of network volumes and ~36% of Card Member loans; risk of loss, renegotiation on worse terms, or partner distress triggering payments or loan sales.
  - Merchant pricing pressure: incentives and concessions to large merchants and aggregators; erosion of average discount rate from regulation and acceptance expansion; merchant-owned payment solutions could compress pricing.
  - Surcharging/steering: permitted in various jurisdictions; differential surcharging and steering can suppress Amex usage and harm coverage, volumes, and brand.
  - Growth investments and rewards: uncertainty over payback of marketing/promotion, rewards, and services; rising costs (inflation, talent, supply chain) may pressure margins; reliance on key redemption partners (e.g., Amazon, Delta).
  - Brand/reputation and ESG: public perceptions of service, data practices, political/social stances, and ESG progress can affect customer/partner relationships; increased scrutiny of ESG disclosures.
  - Cybersecurity/fraud: growing sophistication of attacks, third-party breaches, ransomware, and fraud risks; potential for regulatory action, litigation, brand harm, and reduced usage despite investment and insurance.
  - Operational resilience: technology outages or degradation (internal or third-party) can disrupt processing, reporting, and services, triggering penalties and reputational damage.
  - Third-party reliance: service providers, processors, aggregators, and partners introduce operational, security, compliance, and data governance risks; oversight complexity.
  - Technology evolution: need for sustained investment in data, AI/ML, authentication, tokenization, real-time settlement, and alternative rails; risks of flawed models, biased datasets, governance gaps, or failed adoption.
  - M&A, JVs, and investments: integration, liability, control, regulatory, IP, and reputational risks (including JV in China and GBTG relationship/brand licensing); potential impairments.
  - Talent and culture: attraction/retention challenges, compensation pressures, regulatory oversight of pay, and hybrid work impacts on productivity and culture.
  - Climate transition and physical risks: operational disruption, changing customer behavior, regulatory and disclosure demands, and strategy/technology costs.
- Legal, regulatory and compliance risks:
  - Broad global supervision: evolving, and sometimes divergent, regimes (post-Brexit UK vs EU) can raise costs, restrict products/pricing, and complicate compliance; potential limits on capital actions if requirements not met.
  - Payments regulation: interchange caps and routing rules indirectly pressure discount revenue; EU three-party network rules affect cobrand/agent structures and contributed to exits in the EU and Australia; uncertainty and potential penalties in the EU.
  - AML/CFT: heightened global scrutiny (including in parts of the EU), new products (e.g., checking), and digital assets raise oversight costs and enforcement risk.
  - Consumer protection/data: identity theft, credit reporting, disclosures and marketing oversight may restrict issuance and partnerships; rising privacy, data protection, data transfer/localization, resiliency, third-party oversight, and cybersecurity requirements increase costs and limit data use.
  - Litigation and investigations: exposure to class actions, regulatory inquiries, penalties, restitution, and business changes; ongoing U.S. reviews of historical small business sales practices; potential merchant contract disputes (non-discrimination and honor-all-cards) could force agreement changes and damages.
  - Capital/liquidity rules: potential for higher capital needs (e.g., Basel revisions, stress capital buffer), with constraints on dividends/buybacks; subsidiary dividend limits can affect parent liquidity.
  - IP risks: challenges protecting trade secrets globally and potential third-party infringement claims.
  - Tax risks: audits and disputes (e.g., VAT) and OECD global minimum tax adoption may raise effective tax rate; increased enforcement activity.
- Credit, liquidity and market risks:
  - Risk management/model limitations: frameworks and models (including CECL) may not capture evolving risks; data quality and assumptions may be flawed.
  - Credit risk: exposure across consumer/small business, corporate, merchants, partners, and counterparties; rising 2022 delinquencies/write-offs expected to continue; regulatory constraints can affect collections.
  - Interest rate risk: net interest income sensitivity (e.g., a 100 bps increase estimated to reduce annual NII by ~$141 million as of 12/31/22); higher rates may raise payment burdens and alter revolve behavior; 2022 interest expense ~$2.8B.
  - Funding/liquidity: dependence on capital markets and securitizations; market stress can raise costs or limit access; early amortization risk; ratings downgrades could constrain funding and increase costs.
  - Foreign exchange: ~22% of 2022 revenue outside the U.S.; FX volatility and controls can affect earnings and capital flows.
  - Deposits: growing reliance on AENB deposits; competition and regulatory constraints (e.g., brokered deposit rules, rate caps) may impact ability to attract/retain cost-effective funding.
  - Investment portfolio: valuation and impairment risk for debt and equity holdings (including Amex Ventures) due to market/economic conditions.
- Other items:
  - Item 1B Unresolved Staff Comments: Not applicable.
  - Item 2 Properties: Details principal owned/leased offices (e.g., NYC headquarters, data centers in AZ and NC, global offices) and airport lounge operations.
  - Item 3 Legal Proceedings: Incorporated by reference to Note 12 of the Consolidated Financial Statements.
  - Item 4 Mine Safety Disclosures: Not applicable.

structure.title: Executive Overview
structure.heading: Executive Overview
structure.start_phrase:
We are a globally integrated payments company with four reportable operating segments: U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS),
International Card Services (ICS) and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS).
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: Item 7 MD&A outlines an executive overview and business introduction for a globally integrated payments company operating four segments (U.S. Consumer Services, Commercial Services, International Card Services, and Global Merchant & Network Services), with Corporate & Other for certain functions.
- Offerings and channels: Broad suite of products/services including credit and charge cards, banking/financing, merchant acquiring and processing, network services, fraud prevention, loyalty program design/operation, expense management, and travel/lifestyle services. Distributed via digital and mobile, affiliates, referrals, partners, third-party providers, direct mail/phone, in-house sales, and advertising.
- Revenue model: Five primary sources—discount revenue (largest, tied to merchant discount/acceptance terms), interest income on loans, net card fees (annual membership), service fees and other revenue (FX, travel commissions, delinquency and other fees, equity-method results), and processed revenue (network partnership royalties/fees).
- Non-GAAP and FX: Uses non-GAAP measures, including FX-adjusted metrics to isolate currency impacts; reconciliations referenced.
- 2022 performance highlights (vs. 2021 unless noted): 
  - Total revenues net of interest expense up 25% to $52.9B; network volumes up 21% to $1.55T.
  - Net income down 7% to $7.5B; diluted EPS $9.85; ROE 32.3%; effective tax rate 21.6%.
  - Loans up 22% to $108B; receivables up 7%; cash $33.9B; customer deposits up 31% to $110B; long-term debt up 10%; CET1 ratio 10.3%.
  - Provisions for credit losses increased due to a $617M reserve build vs. a $2.5B release in 2021; delinquencies/write-offs rose but remained below pre‑pandemic levels.
- Business environment and growth drivers: 
  - Strategy momentum with record new card acquisitions, deeper customer relationships, and broader merchant acceptance; strong engagement among Millennial/Gen Z.
  - Billed business up 23% overall (25% FX-adjusted), led by: U.S. Consumer +24%; Commercial +21% (SME strength and corporate recovery); International +23% (+36% FX-adjusted).
  - T&E spend remained strong; Goods & Services growth moderated late in the year. Inflation modestly helped spend; stronger USD weighed on international billings.
- Revenue line trends: 
  - Discount revenue +25%, tracking billed business growth.
  - Net card fees +17% on premium portfolio growth and high retention.
  - Service fees and other revenue +36% on FX-related Card Member spend, higher travel commissions/fees, and more delinquency fees; prior-year included a GBTG non-cash gain.
  - Processed revenue +5% on higher processed volumes, partly offset by prior-year repositioning of alternative payment solutions.
  - Net interest income +28% on higher average loans; rising rates became a modest headwind late in the year. Interest expense rose on higher rates for deposits and debt.
- Expenses and investments: 
  - Rewards, services, and business development rose with volumes and greater use of travel-related benefits; rewards mix skewed more to travel categories.
  - Marketing remained elevated to drive growth and record acquisitions.
  - Operating expenses +24%, driven by Amex Ventures net losses in 2022 vs. gains in 2021 and higher compensation/headcount; ongoing focus on efficiency.
- Capital and shareholder returns: Returned $4.9B via buybacks and dividends; targeting CET1 of 10–11% while supporting balance sheet growth; plans to raise the regular quarterly dividend by 15% beginning Q1 2023.
- Reporting presentation updates (from Q1 2022): 
  - Separated “Processed revenue” from prior categories; combined “Other fees and commissions” and “Other revenue” into “Service fees and other revenue.”
  - Split “Marketing and business development” into distinct “Business development” and “Marketing” lines. Prior periods recast with no impact to totals.
- Risk and outlook references: Notes to supervision/regulation, risk factors, and forward-looking statements highlight potential impacts from macroeconomic, geopolitical, competitive, legal, and regulatory developments.

structure.title: Consolidated Results of Operations
structure.heading: Consolidated Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: The discussions in the “Consolidated Results of Operations” and “Business Segment Results of Operations” provide commentary on the variances for the year ended December 31, 2022 compared to the year ended December 31, 2021, as presented in the accompanying tables.
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: Presents the Consolidated Results of Operations and Business Segment Results, focusing on 2022 vs. 2021; directs readers to the 2021 Form 10‑K for 2021 vs. 2020 comparisons.
- Reporting changes: Recast presentation beginning Q1 2022 to add Processed revenue (separately from Discount revenue/Other), combine residual Other fees and commissions and Other revenue into Service fees and other revenue, and split Marketing and Business development; no impact to total non‑interest revenues or total expenses.
- Revenues: Total revenues net of interest expense rose 25% to $52.9B.
  - Discount revenue up 25% on 23% billed business growth.
  - Net card fees up 17% from premium card portfolio growth.
  - Service fees and other revenue up 36% on FX-related cross‑currency revenues, higher consumer travel commissions/fees, and higher delinquency fees; partially offset by a prior‑year non‑cash GBTG gain.
  - Processed revenue up 5% on higher processed volumes, partly offset by prior‑year alternative payments repositioning.
  - Interest income up 40% on higher average loan balances and rates; interest expense up due to higher rates on deposits and debt.
- Credit provisions: Shifted from a $1.4B reserve release in 2021 to a $2.2B provision in 2022, driven by loan/receivable growth, higher delinquencies, and macroeconomic forecast changes, partially offset by releasing pandemic‑era reserves; “Other” provisions increased due to net reserve build on non‑card loans.
- Expenses: Total expenses increased 24% to $41.1B.
  - Card Member rewards up 27% (higher Membership Rewards and cash back, greater spend in higher‑earn categories like travel, and higher cobrand rewards; URR 96%).
  - Business development up 31% (partner payments and client incentives on higher network volumes).
  - Card Member services up 48% (greater usage of travel benefits).
  - Marketing up 3% (growth investments and new card acquisitions).
  - Salaries and benefits up 16% (larger colleague base and compensation actions).
  - Other expenses up 35% (net losses on Amex Ventures versus prior‑year gains).
- Taxes: Effective tax rate declined to 21.6% from 24.6%, reflecting discrete benefits from resolution of prior‑year tax items and the relationship of pretax income to recurring permanent benefits and geographic mix.
- Card and network metrics:
  - Network volumes +21%; billed business +23%; processed volumes +10%.
  - Cards‑in‑force +10% (proprietary +7%); basic cards‑in‑force +11%.
  - Average proprietary basic spend +15%; average discount rate 2.34% (vs. 2.30%); average fee per card $82 (vs. $74).
  - By category: G&S billed business +13%; T&E +64% (airlines +119%). FX‑adjusted growth rates higher than reported where noted.
- Credit quality and balances:
  - Card Member loans $108B (+22%); reserves $3.75B (3.5% of loans); net write‑off rate (principal only) 0.9%; 30+ DPD 1.0%.
  - Card Member receivables $57.6B (+7%); reserves $229M (0.4% of receivables); net write‑off rate 0.8%.
- Net interest yield: Adjusted net interest income $10.14B; net interest yield on average Card Member loans 10.6% (non‑GAAP measure explained alongside GAAP net interest income per average loans).
- Segment reporting: Realigned reportable segments in Q3 2022 to USCS, CS, ICS, and GMNS; Corporate & Other houses corporate functions and certain other operations. Describes allocation methodologies:
  - Revenues: Discount revenue allocated via transfer pricing; net card fees and processed revenue directly to segments; interest/fees on loans directly to segments; interest expense allocated via internal funding.
  - Provisions: Direct to segments.
  - Expenses: Rewards and services direct; business development and marketing largely direct; global brand advertising allocated by revenue; shared service and overhead allocated by activity and relative revenue/loan/receivable levels.

structure.title: Business Segment Results of Operations
structure.heading: Business Segment Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase: We consider a combination of factors when evaluating the composition of our reportable operating segments, including the results reviewed by the chief operating decision maker, economic characteristics, products and services offered, classes of customers, product distribution channels, geographic considerations (primarily United States versus outside the United States) and regulatory considerations.
structure.summary:
- Explains the company’s reportable operating segments, the 2022 realignment (USCS, CS, ICS, GMNS, and Corporate & Other), and how management allocates revenues, interest expense, credit loss provisions, and operating expenses across segments.
- Details revenue allocation methodologies (e.g., discount revenue split between issuer and network components, direct attribution of net card fees and interest on loans, internal transfer pricing for funding costs).
- Describes expense allocation (actual segment-incurred rewards, services, business development, and marketing; allocation of global brand advertising; service and overhead cost allocations).
- U.S. Consumer Services (USCS): Strong 2022 revenue growth driven by higher discount revenue from a 24% increase in billed business, rising net card fees, travel-related service fees, and loan-driven net interest income; higher provisions due to reserve builds and rising delinquencies; expense increases led by rewards, travel-related benefits, partner payments, marketing, and compensation; includes key portfolio statistics (billed business, cards-in-force, loans, delinquencies, write-offs, and net interest yield).
- Commercial Services (CS): Revenue growth led by discount revenue from increased commercial billed business, higher net card fees, and FX-related service fees; processed revenue declined due to a prior-year business repositioning; higher provisions from reserve builds and net write-offs; expenses up on rewards, client incentives, travel benefits, marketing, and compensation; includes segment statistics (billed business, cards-in-force, loans/receivables metrics, and net interest yield).
- International Card Services (ICS): Revenue growth across categories (notably discount revenue and service fees) but lower pretax income due to U.S. dollar strength; higher provisions from reserve builds and write-offs; expenses up on rewards and a joint venture-related charge in business development; marketing flat on an FX-adjusted basis; includes international portfolio statistics and FX-adjusted references.
- Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS): Revenue growth driven by discount revenue from higher billed business, increased service fees (FX-related), and processed revenue; net interest income benefited from an interest expense credit tied to larger merchant payables and higher rates; modest expense growth from compensation and partner payments; significant increase in pretax income; provides network volume and asset data.
- Corporate & Other: Larger pretax loss in 2022 due to Amex Ventures net losses (vs. prior-year gains), prior-year non-cash gain related to GBTG, and higher compensation costs.
- Consolidated capital resources and liquidity: Objectives to maintain a strong equity capital profile, diversified funding, and robust liquidity to cover at least 12 months under stress; capital strategy to support growth and return excess capital (dividends/share repurchases); regulatory framework under Basel III with a CET1 target of 10–11%; internal capital adequacy process; flexibility to shift capital among subsidiaries; acknowledgment of capital market volatility and corresponding balance sheet management.

structure.title: Consolidated Capital Resources and Liquidity
structure.heading: Consolidated Capital Resources and Liquidity
structure.start_phrase: Our balance sheet management objectives are to maintain:
structure.summary:
- Corporate & Other: Reported pretax loss of $2.2B in 2022 vs. $1.0B in 2021, driven by Amex Ventures investment losses (vs. prior-year gains), a prior-year non-cash gain from GBTG equity value increase, and higher compensation costs.
- Capital resources and strategy: Objectives to maintain strong equity, diversified funding, and 12+ months of liquidity under stress. Capital allocated to businesses exceeding cost of capital; retain capital to support growth and return excess via dividends and buybacks. Target CET1 ratio of 10–11%; flexibility to shift capital across subsidiaries; Basel III standardized approach; subject to U.S. bank regulatory capital requirements.
- Regulatory capital and ratios (12/31/22): AmEx Co. CET1 10.3%, Tier 1 11.1%, Total 12.8%, Leverage 9.9%; AENB CET1 11.3%, Tier 1 11.3%, Total 13.2%, Leverage 9.7%. Capital components: CET1 $20.0B, Tier 1 $21.6B, Tier 2 $3.3B, Total $24.9B; RWA $194.4B; average assets for leverage $218.6B. CECL capital impact phased in (50% as of 1/1/23). $1.6B preferred outstanding; Tier 2 includes $870M eligible subordinated notes.
- Stress testing: Category IV firm; 2022 Fed SCB confirmed at 2.5%, establishing 7% minimum CET1 effective 10/1/22.
- Capital return: 2022 distributions of $4.9B (dividends $1.6B; share repurchases $3.3B, 20M shares at $168.14), ~64% of capital generated; planned 15% increase in quarterly dividend to $0.60 starting Q1 2023; $57M preferred dividends. Repurchase methods may include open market, 10b5-1, block, ASRs.
- Funding strategy and programs: Diversified sources across deposits, unsecured debt, securitizations, secured facilities, and a committed bank credit facility; balanced maturity profile; expected deposit growth. Year-end 2022: deposits $110.2B (vs. $84.4B 2021), short-term borrowings $1.3B (vs. $2.2B), long-term debt $42.6B (vs. $38.7B). 2023 plan includes $6–10B unsecured and $5–9B secured term issuance.
- Credit ratings: Generally A2/A-/A long-term and P-1/A-2/F1 short-term across key entities; stable outlooks; note potential impacts of downgrades mitigated by FDIC-insured retail deposit mix.
- Deposits: FDIC-insured deposits at AENB via direct high-yield savings and CDs, checking, and third-party channels; deposit-gathering linked to AENB capital levels.
- Short-term funding: Used mainly for working capital; no commercial paper outstanding in 2022.
- Long-term debt and securitization: $42.6B long-term debt outstanding; periodic securitizations of card loans/receivables via trusts. 2022 issuances totaled $20.5B, including fixed, floating (SOFR-based), fixed-to-floating senior and subordinated notes, and trust Class A certificates.
- Liquidity management: Maintain diversified on/off-balance sheet liquidity, unencumbered liquid assets, and committed facilities; stress testing across multiple scenarios; recognize potential NII drag from liquidity.
- Contingent liquidity: Two undrawn secured borrowing facilities ($3.0B Charge Trust, maturing 7/15/24; $2.0B Lending Trust, maturing 9/16/24). Access to Fed discount window via AENB; ~$102.8B of U.S. card loans/receivables potentially pledgeable/securitizable. Undrawn $3.5B syndicated bank credit facility (matures 10/15/24) with CET1-based conditions; can backstop commercial paper.
- Off-balance sheet arrangements: Include guarantees, indemnifications, and certain Card Member/partner arrangements.
- Cash flows: 2022—operating $21.1B provided (driven by net income and higher merchant payables/Membership Rewards liability), investing $(33.7)B used (higher loans/receivables and securities purchases), financing $24.5B provided (deposit growth and net debt issuance offset by buybacks/dividends). 2021—operating $14.6B provided, investing $(10.5)B used, financing $(14.9)B used; drivers explained.
- Risk management governance: Enterprise-wide Risk Management led by CRO, overseen by Board committees. Risk Committee oversees ERM framework, risk appetite, major risk types, capital/liquidity standards, and ICAAP/CCAR. Audit & Compliance Committee oversees compliance program, financial reporting integrity, internal/external audit, and internal controls. Compensation & Benefits Committee aligns incentives with risk, uses risk-balanced compensation framework with CRO input.

structure.title: Risk Management
structure.heading: Risk Management
structure.start_phrase: We use our comprehensive Enterprise-wide Risk Management (ERM) program to identify, aggregate, monitor, measure, report and manage risks.
structure.summary:
- Overview of Enterprise-wide Risk Management (ERM): Company-wide framework led by the Chief Risk Officer to identify, measure, monitor, report and manage risks; defines risk appetite, governance, culture and capabilities.

- Board governance: Oversight via three independent Board committees.
  - Risk Committee: Oversees ERM framework, sets risk appetite, covers all major risk types (credit, operational, compliance, reputational, market, funding/liquidity, model, strategic/business, country, ESG). Reviews risk profile, capital/liquidity standards, ICAAP/CCAR, and CRO performance.
  - Audit and Compliance Committee: Oversees financial reporting integrity, internal controls, external auditor independence, and the Internal Audit Group; approves compliance policies and evaluates the Compliance Risk Management Program.
  - Compensation and Benefits Committee: Ensures compensation balances risk and performance; works with CRO on risk goals and uses a risk-balanced incentive framework.

- Management committees and structure:
  - ERMC (chaired by CRO): Highest management risk body; maintains risk appetite framework, oversees policy implementation, limits, exposures, trends and concentrations.
  - Asset Liability Committee (chaired by CFO): Manages capital, funding, liquidity, investments, market risk and ALM.
  - Three lines of defense: 1st line (business leaders/CFO), 2nd line (Risk, Compliance, Operational Risk, control groups), 3rd line (Internal Audit).

- Credit risk management:
  - Individual credit risk: Consumer/small business cards and loans; managed via ICRC, dedicated Chief Credit Officers, and proprietary scoring/decision models; correlated with macro factors like unemployment and GDP.
  - Institutional credit risk: Lower frequency/higher severity exposures in CS, ICS, GMNS, investment and liquidity activities; overseen by IRMC and Chief Credit Officers; centralized risk ratings; focus on underwriting standards, monitoring, and risk-adjusted returns.
  - Airline and travel exposure: Significant partnerships (notably Delta) and broader travel relationships assessed under ERM; highlights potential partner and concentration risks.
  - Debt exposure monitoring: Country, sector, and counterparty concentration oversight; high-risk country exposures evaluated and considered not material as of Dec 31, 2022.

- Operational risk management:
  - Framework governed by the Operational Risk Management Policy and ORMC; components include event capture, issue management, key risk indicators, and process/entity-level assessments; focus on root-cause analysis, customer remediation, control enhancement.
  - Information and cyber security: Program aligned to NIST CSF with ongoing investments; risks highlighted in risk factors.
  - Information technology risk: Policies and controls to ensure system stability, resilience and availability.
  - Privacy: Global Privacy Policy and Privacy Risk Management Committee; governance over personal data processing.
  - Data management and governance: Enterprise Data Governance Policy; Enterprise Data Committee chaired by Chief Data Officer.
  - Third-party risk: Board- and ERMC-approved policy; lifecycle management across due diligence, contracting, monitoring, and termination.
  - Conduct risk: Policy and Conduct Risk Committee govern assessments, controls, training, escalation, and consequence management.

- Compliance risk management:
  - Global Compliance and Ethics runs the corporate-wide Compliance Risk Management Program; CRMC (dual reports to ERMC and Audit & Compliance Committee) oversees identification and escalation.
  - Robust Anti-Money Laundering program with independent rule assessments and Internal Audit reviews.

- Reputational risk: Embedded in business decision-making; ERMC ensures consideration across policies and escalations.

- Market risk management:
  - Policies and limits overseen by ERMC/ALCO/Market Risk Management Committee; independent oversight via Market Risk Oversight Officer.
  - Interest rate risk: Scenario analysis and use of swaps; a 100 bp immediate increase estimated to reduce annual net interest income by ~$141 million as of Dec 31, 2022.
  - Foreign exchange risk: Managed via spot and forward hedges; ~$34B notional FX derivatives outstanding as of Dec 31, 2022. A 10% USD strengthening was generally immaterial for card/cross-currency and translation exposures, but would reduce next-12-month pretax income by ~$153 million.
  - Limited market risk from Foreign Exchange International Payments, mitigated through hedging and limits.

- Funding and liquidity risk management:
  - Board-approved Liquidity Risk Policy; Funding and Liquidity Committee manages diversified liquidity resources to meet obligations for at least 12 months under severe stress; oversight at consolidated and key subsidiary levels; normal and stressed funding plans and monitoring.

- Model risk management:
  - Enterprise-Wide Model Risk Policy (approved by ERMC) covering development, independent validation, reporting, change management and ongoing performance; enhanced oversight of AI/ML models to mitigate adverse outcomes.

- Strategic and business risk:
  - Governance over strategic decisions, M&A and product changes through Executive Committee diligence, CRO/risk committee approvals, and New Products Committee; periodic performance reviews.

- Country risk management:
  - Policies to monitor, control and escalate exposures based on economic, social and political conditions.

- ESG and climate-related risk:
  - Treated as cross-cutting and identified as an emerging risk; focus on transition and physical risks and ongoing risk identification within governance.

- Critical accounting estimates—Reserves for Card Member credit losses (CECL):
  - Lifetime expected credit losses estimated using historical loss experience plus current and forecasted economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable period (~3 years), then revert to long-term averages.
  - Quantitative models estimate probability of default, exposure at default, and recoveries; qualitative overlays capture emerging trends.
  - Assumptions on allocation of future payments to interest/fees, future spend, and remaining balances for revolving loans.
  - Multiple third-party macroeconomic scenarios (e.g., unemployment, real GDP) weighted by management judgment each period.

structure.title: Critical Accounting Estimates
structure.heading: Critical Accounting Estimates
structure.start_phrase: Refer to Note 1 to the “Consolidated Financial Statements” for a summary of our significant accounting policies.
structure.summary:
- Overview of critical accounting estimates, with detailed policies and judgments underpinning:
  - Reserves for Card Member credit losses under CECL (effective Jan 1, 2020): modeling lifetime expected losses using historical data plus current and forecasted economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable (R&S) period of about three years; immediate reversion to long-term average loss rates beyond the R&S period; receivables assumed paid or written off by 180 days past due. Key modeling judgments include probability of default, exposure at default (including allocation of future payments across interest/fees, future spend, and existing balances), expected recoveries, and macroeconomic scenario weightings (unemployment, real GDP). Management applies qualitative overlays based on emerging portfolio trends.
  - Macroeconomic sensitivity illustration: as of December 31, 2022, every 10 percentage point shift in weighting from a baseline to a pessimistic downside scenario increased modeled estimated credit losses by approximately $120 million; results are scenario- and assumption-dependent and exclude management judgment overlays in qualitative reserves.
  - Membership Rewards liability: methodology based on Ultimate Redemption Rate (URR) and Weighted Average Cost (WAC) per point for current enrollees; URR estimated via statistical/actuarial models using redemption trends, product type, tenure, spend, and credit attributes; WAC derived from trailing 12-month redemptions and adjusted for expected cost/pattern changes. Sensitivities as of December 31, 2022: +25 bps URR increases liability/expense by ~$157 million; +1 bp WAC per point increases liability/expense by ~$190 million.
  - Goodwill recoverability: annual or trigger-based impairment testing with an optional qualitative screen; quantitative valuations combine income (discounted cash flows using CAPM-based cost of equity and terminal growth) and market (comparable multiples) approaches; results sensitive to assumptions on cash flows, discount rates, and market comparables.
  - Income taxes: accounting for unrecognized tax benefits using a more-likely-than-not recognition threshold and largest-benefit measurement; ongoing reassessment as new information emerges. Deferred tax assets evaluated for realization based on projected taxable income, reversing temporary differences, and tax planning strategies; reassessed quarterly.

- Other matters: internal review identified some current and former U.S. Card Members with multiple cards were not credited certain earned Membership Rewards points; review completed in Q4 2022 with an immaterial impact on 2022 financial statements.

- Recently issued and adopted accounting standards: referenced to Note 1 of the Consolidated Financial Statements.

- Glossary of selected terminology: definitions for key business and reporting terms, including adjusted net interest income, airline-related volume, asset securitizations (and on-balance-sheet trust treatment), average discount rate, billed business, capital ratios, Card Member, Card Member loans vs. receivables, cards-in-force (and exclusions), and charge cards (including Pay Over Time and Plan It features).

structure.title: Other Matters
structure.heading: Other Matters
structure.start_phrase:
As previously disclosed, we identified during an internal review that over time certain current and former U.S. Card Members with multiple cards were not
credited certain Membership Rewards points that they had earned.
structure.summary:
- Other Matters: Internal review found some U.S. Card Members with multiple cards were not credited certain earned Membership Rewards points; review completed in Q4 2022 with an immaterial impact on 2022 financial statements.
- Recently Issued/Adopted Accounting Standards: Points readers to Note 1 for details.
- Glossary of Selected Terminology: Provides definitions of key operating and financial terms used throughout the report, including:
  - Revenue/volume metrics: discount revenue, average discount rate, billed business, network volumes, processed revenue/volumes, G&S-related and T&E-related volumes.
  - Customer/product metrics: Card Member, cards-in-force, charge vs. credit cards, cobrand cards.
  - Credit/risk measures: Card Member loans/receivables, net write-off rates (principal-only and principal/interest/fees), reserve build/release, capital ratios.
  - Interest measures: interest income/expense components, adjusted net interest income, net interest yield on average Card Member loans.
  - Other: asset securitizations, loyalty coalitions, net card fees, operating expenses.
- Cautionary Note Regarding Forward-Looking Statements: Outlines numerous risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ, including:
  - Macroeconomic and geopolitical conditions (inflation, interest rates, recession risk, labor markets, supply chains, energy costs, COVID-19 effects, Russia-Ukraine conflict).
  - Revenue growth sustainability; merchant discount rate dynamics; competition and pricing pressure; product innovation and cobrand agreements.
  - Net card fees performance; net interest income, loan growth, and rate effects; credit performance, delinquencies, reserves, and write-offs.
  - Marketing spend effectiveness; rewards, services, and business development costs; operating expense control amid inflation and talent costs.
  - Tax rate volatility; capital return plans (dividends/buybacks) and regulatory capital/stress testing.
  - Strategic execution: premium consumer and commercial payments leadership, merchant coverage expansion (including OptBlue), technology/digital and AI capabilities, international growth.

structure.title: Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm (PCAOB ID 238)

structure.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheets of American Express Company and its subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and the related consolidated statements of income, of comprehensive income, of shareholders’ equity and of cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December 31, 2022, including the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”).

- Change in accounting principle noted: adoption of new credit loss standard (CECL) in 2020.
- Basis for opinions: management’s responsibilities; auditor independence and PCAOB compliance; audit scope and procedures for financial statements and internal controls.
- Definition and inherent limitations of internal control over financial reporting.
- Critical audit matters:
  - Reserves for credit losses on Card Member loans ($3.7B at 12/31/22): complex judgments around reasonable and supportable period, probability/exposure at default, economic conditions, recoveries, and qualitative overlays; use of models and specialists; testing of controls, inputs, methodology, and assumptions.
  - Membership Rewards liability ($12.8B at 12/31/22): key assumptions include Ultimate Redemption Rate (URR) and Weighted Average Cost (WAC) per point; statistical/actuarial modeling, inputs such as redemption trends, product type, tenure, spend levels; testing of controls, data completeness/accuracy, independent estimation and comparison.
- Auditor details: signed in New York, dated February 10, 2023; auditor of the company since 2005.
- Index to Consolidated Financial Statements:

structure.title: Consolidated Financial Statements
structure.heading: Consolidated Financial Statements
structure.summary:
- Scope: Consolidated financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020, plus the opening notes to the financial statements.
- Consolidated Statements of Income:
  - Revenue mix and totals: Strong growth in non-interest revenues (discount revenue, net card fees, service fees, processed revenue) with total revenues net of interest expense rising to $52.9B in 2022 (from $42.4B in 2021 and $36.1B in 2020).
  - Interest income/expense: Higher interest income in 2022 alongside increased interest expense, yielding net interest income of $9.9B (up from $7.8B in 2021).
  - Credit costs: Provisions for credit losses increased to $2.2B in 2022, versus a net reserve release in 2021 and elevated provisions in 2020.
  - Operating expenses: Significant increases in card member rewards, business development, services, marketing, and salaries/benefits in 2022.
  - Earnings: Pretax income of $9.6B and net income of $7.5B in 2022 (down from $8.1B in 2021, up from $3.1B in 2020). Basic/Diluted EPS of $9.86/$9.85 in 2022; share count declined year over year. EPS footnote reflects allocations to participating awards and preferred dividends.
- Consolidated Statements of Comprehensive Income:
  - OCI drivers: Net unrealized losses on debt securities, negative foreign currency translation adjustments, and positive pension/OPEB adjustments.
  - Comprehensive income totaled $7.2B in 2022 (down from $8.0B in 2021).
- Consolidated Balance Sheets (2022 vs. 2021):
  - Assets: Total assets grew to $228.4B from $188.5B, driven by higher cash and cash equivalents, card member receivables and loans, and investment securities; includes disclosure of reserves and VIE-related amounts.
  - Liabilities: Customer deposits increased to $110.2B; long-term debt rose; other liabilities up.
  - Equity: Shareholders’ equity increased to $24.7B; AOCI more negative; common shares outstanding declined; preferred shares line shows none outstanding at year-end.
- Consolidated Statements of Cash Flows:
  - Operating activities: Net cash provided rose to $21.1B in 2022, reflecting higher earnings and working capital changes.
  - Investing activities: Net cash used of $33.7B in 2022 due to growth in card member loans/receivables and capex; securities activity detailed.
  - Financing activities: Net cash provided of $24.5B in 2022, driven by deposit growth and long-term debt issuance; includes share repurchases and dividends; prior-year preferred share issuance/redemption noted.
  - Supplemental reconciliation of restricted cash included.
- Consolidated Statements of Shareholders’ Equity (2019–2022 rollforward):
  - Tracks net income, OCI, share repurchases, issuances, preferred share activity (issuance and redemption in 2021), and dividends.
  - Notes the cumulative CECL adoption impact in 2020 reducing retained earnings.
  - Ending 2022 equity: $24.7B; highlights increased common dividends and ongoing buybacks.
- Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements (partial):
  - Company overview: A globally integrated payments company offering credit/charge cards, travel, and lifestyle services to consumers and businesses via multiple distribution channels and segments.
  - Principles of consolidation: GAAP basis; elimination of intercompany transactions; consolidation of entities with controlling financial interests, including VIEs where the company is the primary beneficiary; equity method for significant influence; measurement of certain equity investments at fair value through earnings.
  - Foreign currency: Transaction gains/losses recognized in earnings; translation adjustments for non-USD functional subsidiaries recorded in AOCI, with reclassification upon disposal or substantial liquidation of foreign operations.

nodes.heading: 1.3 FOREIGN CURRENCY
nodes.start_phrase: Transactions conducted in currencies other than the applicable functional currency of an entity are converted to the functional currency at the exchange rate on the transaction date.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements — Note 1: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies.
- Company overview: A globally integrated payments company offering credit and charge cards plus travel and lifestyle services to consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations worldwide through multiple channels. Segment details referenced in Note 24; certain activities in Corporate & Other.
- Principles of consolidation: Financials prepared under U.S. GAAP with intercompany eliminations. Consolidation of entities where the company has a controlling financial interest—via voting control or as primary beneficiary of VIEs (power and benefits/losses potentially significant). Equity method for significant influence investments. Non-public equity investments recorded at cost and adjusted to fair value for observable price changes or impairment; marketable equity securities policy referenced in Note 4.
- Foreign currency: Transactions remeasured at transaction/period-end rates with gains/losses in Other, net expenses. Translation of foreign subsidiaries at period-end/average rates with adjustments (including qualifying hedge and tax effects) recorded in AOCI and reclassified to earnings upon disposal or substantial liquidation of foreign operations.
- Use of estimates: Significant estimates include reserves for Card Member credit losses on loans/receivables, Membership Rewards liability, goodwill, and income taxes; actual results may differ.
- Revenue recognition (income statement):
  - General: Revenue recognized upon satisfaction of performance obligations. Disclosure exemptions for contracts with original expected duration ≤1 year and variable consideration; non-interest revenue expected in future periods for other contracts is not material.
  - Discount revenue: Fees retained from merchants for facilitating card transactions; rate varies by merchant factors (industry, volume, payment method, settlement terms, submission method, geography, transaction size). Recognized at transaction time. Merchant contracts range from open-ended (SMB) to 3–7 years (large merchants), often with auto-renewal; obligations satisfied over the term through network services. For third-party acquirers (e.g., OptBlue, certain network partners), a negotiated network rate is recognized as discount revenue at transaction time.
  - Net card fees: Annual membership fees (net of acquisition costs and refund reserves) deferred and recognized straight-line over 12 months; unamortized balance in Other liabilities.
  - Service fees and other revenue: Includes merchant/customer service fees, travel commissions/fees (recognized when services performed), delinquency and FX-related fees (recognized when charged), and equity-method investment income/losses (see Note 18).
  - Processed revenue: Revenues from network partnership agreements (royalties, fees, and facilitation of partner-issued card transactions). The company settles with merchants/acquirers; fees deducted and recognized at transaction time. Issuer rate paid to partners is recorded as contra-revenue up to revenue from the same customer; any excess recorded in Business development expense. Includes fees from alternative payment solutions, recognized when services are performed.

nodes.title: AMOUNTS BASED ON ESTIMATES AND ASSUMPTIONS

- Service fees and other revenue: service fees, travel commissions recognized when services are performed; delinquency and foreign currency-related fees recognized when charged; includes equity-method income/losses.
- Processed revenue: income from network partnership agreements (royalties, fees, transaction facilitation); merchant discount captured and recognized at transaction time; issuer rate recorded as contra-revenue to the extent of related customer revenue, with any excess recorded as Business development expense; includes fees from alternative payment solutions recognized when services are performed.

nodes.title: INCOME STATEMENT - Introduction

INCOME STATEMENT
Revenue is recognized when obligations under the terms of a contract with our customers are satisfied. We are not required to disclose revenue that is expected
to be recognized in future periods related to contracts that have an original expected duration of one year or less and contracts with variable consideration (e.g.,
discount revenue). Non-interest revenue expected to be recognized in future periods related to all other contracts with customers is not material.

nodes.title: Discount Revenue
nodes.heading: 1.5.1 Discount Revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Discount revenue represents the amount we earn and retain from the merchant payable for facilitating transactions between Card Members and merchants on payment products issued by American Express.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on accounting estimates and assumptions used in the Consolidated Financial Statements, noting key areas subject to management judgment: reserves for Card Member credit losses, Membership Rewards liability, goodwill, and income taxes, with a caution that actual results may differ.
- Revenue recognition policy: revenue recognized when contractual performance obligations are satisfied; disclosure exemptions for contracts with original duration of one year or less and for variable consideration; future-period non‑interest revenue from other contracts deemed not material.
- Discount revenue: earned from merchant discount fees for facilitating Card Member–merchant transactions; fee levels vary by merchant/industry/volume/methods/terms/geography/transaction size; recognized at transaction time. Merchant contract structures differ (SMB often open‑ended; large merchants typically 3–7 years with possible auto‑renewals); obligations fulfilled over the contract term via daily processing/network availability. For third‑party acquirers (e.g., OptBlue, network partners), a negotiated network rate fee is recognized as discount revenue at transaction time.
- Net card fees: annual membership fees (net of acquisition costs and projected refund reserves) are deferred and recognized straight‑line over the 12‑month membership period; considered relatively stable; unamortized balances recorded in Other liabilities.
- Service fees and other revenue: includes merchant/customer service fees and travel commissions (recognized when services are performed), delinquency and foreign currency fees (recognized when charged), and results from equity‑method investments.
- Processed revenue: arises from network partnership agreements (royalties, fees, and facilitation of network partner–issued card transactions). American Express settles with merchants/acquirers on behalf of partners; fees deducted from settlements and recognized at transaction time. Issuer rates paid to partners are recorded as contra‑revenue within Processed revenue to the extent offsettable, with any excess recorded as Business development expense. Also includes fees from alternative payment solutions, recognized when services are performed.
