- Explains Service fees and other revenue: includes merchant and customer service fees and travel commissions (recognized when services are performed), delinquency and foreign currency fees (recognized when charged), and equity method investment income/losses.
- Covers Processed revenue: primarily from network partnership agreements (royalties, fees, and facilitation of partner-issued card transactions). As network operator, the company settles with merchants/acquirers; fees are deducted and recognized at transaction time. Issuer rates paid to partners are recorded as contra-revenue within Processed revenue up to related revenue, with any excess recognized as Business development expense. Also includes fees from alternative payment solutions recognized when services are performed.

nodes.title: Processed Revenue
nodes.heading: 1.5.4 Processed Revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Processed revenue primarily represents revenues related to network partnership agreements, comprising royalties, fees and amounts earned for facilitating transactions on cards issued by network partners.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on accounting estimates and management assumptions used in the Consolidated Financial Statements, with key areas including credit loss reserves, Membership Rewards liabilities, goodwill, and income taxes; acknowledgment that actual results may differ from estimates.
- Revenue recognition principles: revenue recorded when performance obligations are satisfied; exemptions from disclosing future revenue for short-duration or variable consideration contracts; future non-interest revenue from other contracts deemed not material.
- Discount revenue: fees retained from merchants for facilitating card transactions; pricing varies by merchant factors and terms; recognized at transaction time; merchant contracts range from no fixed term (smaller merchants) to 3–7 years (larger merchants) with possible auto-renewal; network rate fees from third-party acquirers (e.g., OptBlue) recognized as discount revenue at transaction time.
- Net card fees: annual membership fees (net of acquisition costs and projected refund reserves) deferred and recognized straight-line over 12 months; unamortized amounts recorded in Other liabilities.
- Service fees and other revenue: includes merchant/customer service fees, travel commissions (recognized when services performed), delinquency and FX-related fees (recognized when charged), and equity-method investment results.
- Processed revenue: network partnership royalties/fees and amounts for facilitating transactions on partner-issued cards; merchant discount recorded as processed revenue at transaction time; issuer rate treated as contra-revenue up to related revenue, with excess recorded as Business development expense; includes fees from alternative payment solutions recognized when services are performed.
- Contra-revenue: payments to merchants, network partners, and other customers recorded as reductions of revenue unless received goods/services have determinable fair value, in which case they are expensed.
- Interest income: on Card Member loans via average daily balance (accrued unless non-accrual); on investment securities via effective interest method until default/likely non-payment; on bank deposits recognized as earned.
- Interest expense: incurred for funding loans/receivables and general liquidity; categorized into deposits and debt; includes realized effects of interest rate hedges on long-term debt.
- Card Member rewards: expense recognized as rewards are earned through spending; liabilities recorded for expected redemptions and point costs (Membership Rewards, cash back) and for cobrand spending with payments to partners; cobrand partners deliver rewards; liabilities vary with enrollment, attrition, earn/redemption volumes, and redemption costs; changes flow through rewards expense.
- Business development: payments to cobrand partners, corporate client incentives tied to targets, and certain network partner payments; expensed as incurred.
- Card Member services: costs of value-added benefits and services; expensed as incurred.
- Marketing: advertising costs expensed when first run; all other marketing costs expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Contra-revenue
nodes.heading: 1.5.5 Contra-revenue
nodes.start_phrase: Payments made pursuant to contractual arrangements with our merchants, network partners, and other customers are classified as contra-revenue, except where we receive goods, services or other benefits for which the fair value is determinable and measurable, in which case they are recorded as expense.
nodes.summary:
- Defines contra-revenue: payments to merchants, network partners, and customers are recorded as contra-revenue unless tied to measurable goods/services, which are expensed.
- Interest income policies: 
  - Card Member loans accrue interest via the average daily balance method until paid off, written off, or placed on non-accrual.
  - Investment securities use the effective interest method until default or when future interest is unlikely.
  - Bank deposits and similar placements recognize interest as earned.
- Interest expense: recognized as incurred, primarily for funding loans/receivables and liquidity, categorized into deposits and debt, and includes the realized impact of interest rate hedging on long-term debt.
- Card Member rewards: expense recognized as rewards are earned; liabilities recorded for expected redemptions and point costs (Membership Rewards, cash back) and for cobrand rewards on spending with payments to partners; liability levels affected by enrollment, attrition, earning/redemption volumes, and costs; changes flow through rewards expense.
- Business development: includes payments to cobrand partners, client incentive payments tied to targets, and certain network partner payments; generally expensed as incurred.
- Card Member services: costs of value-added benefits/services to card members; expensed as incurred.
- Marketing: advertising development and initial placement costs expensed when first run; other marketing costs expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Interest Income
nodes.heading: 1.5.6 Interest Income
nodes.start_phrase: Interest on Card Member loans is assessed using the average daily balance method.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines accounting policies for a payment card company. It covers: (1) contra-revenue, classifying payments to merchants, network partners, and customers as reductions of revenue unless a measurable benefit is received, in which case they are expenses; (2) interest income recognition on Card Member loans using the average daily balance method and on investment securities via the effective interest method, with recognition ceasing on default/non-accrual, plus interest on bank deposits as earned; (3) interest expense incurred to fund loans/receivables and for liquidity, split between deposits and debt, including realized hedge impacts; (4) Card Member rewards, recognizing expense as rewards are earned, recording liabilities for expected redemptions and costs (Membership Rewards and cash back), and for cobrands recording liabilities and payments to partners who provide the rewards, with changes flowing through income; (5) business development costs (cobrand partner payments, corporate client incentives tied to targets, network partner payments) generally expensed as incurred; (6) Card Member services costs for value-added benefits, expensed as incurred; and (7) marketing costs, with ad development/initial placement expensed when first run and other marketing costs expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Interest Expense
nodes.heading: 1.5.7 Interest Expense
nodes.start_phrase: Interest expense includes interest incurred primarily to fund Card Member loans and receivables, general corporate purposes and liquidity needs, and is recognized as incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Contra-revenue: Payments to merchants, network partners, and other customers are recorded as contra-revenue unless specific goods/services with determinable fair value are received, in which case they are expensed.
- Interest income: 
  - Card Member loans accrue interest via the average daily balance method until paid off or written off, except when on non-accrual.
  - Investment securities use the effective interest method; recognition stops at default or when future payments are unlikely.
  - Interest on bank deposits is recognized as earned on time deposits, sweep accounts, and other interest-bearing accounts.
- Interest expense: Recognized as incurred, primarily to fund loans/receivables and for liquidity; categorized into deposits (customer/institution deposits) and debt (short- and long-term borrowings), including realized hedge impacts on long-term debt.
- Card Member rewards: Expense recognized when rewards are earned through spending. Liabilities recorded for expected redemptions and point costs (Membership Rewards, cash back); for cobrand, liabilities reflect rewards on spend and payments to partners, with the partner providing rewards. Liability changes flow through rewards expense.
- Business development: Includes payments to cobrand partners, client incentive payments tied to targets, and certain network partner payments; generally expensed as incurred.
- Card Member services: Costs of value-added benefits and services to Card Members; expensed as incurred.
- Marketing: Advertising development and initial placement costs expensed when first run; other marketing costs generally expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Card Member Rewards
nodes.heading: 1.5.8 Card Member Rewards
nodes.start_phrase: We issue charge and credit cards that allow Card Members to participate in various rewards programs (e.g., Membership Rewards, cash back and cobrand).
nodes.summary:
- Outlines accounting treatment for contra-revenue, classifying payments to merchants, network partners, and customers as contra-revenue unless measurable goods/services are received, in which case they’re expensed.
- Details interest income recognition:
  - Card Member loans: average daily balance method; accrue per account terms until paid or written off; non-accrual exceptions.
  - Investment securities: effective interest method, recognizing premiums/discounts and fees; stop accruing upon default or likely missed payments.
  - Bank deposits and other interest-bearing accounts: recognized as earned.
- Describes interest expense recognition for funding loans/receivables and liquidity:
  - Categorized into deposits (customer/institution deposits) and debt (long-term, short-term, and hedging impacts).
- Explains Card Member rewards accounting:
  - Expense recognized as rewards are earned via spending.
  - Liabilities recorded for expected redemptions (Membership Rewards, cash back) and for cobrand rewards on spending, with payments to partners; partner provides the rewards.
  - Liabilities vary with enrollment, attrition, earn/redemption volumes, and redemption costs; changes flow through rewards expense.
- Defines business development expense: payments to cobrand partners, corporate client incentives, and certain network partner payments; generally expensed as incurred.
- Defines Card Member services expense: costs of value-added benefits and services; expensed as incurred.
- Defines marketing expense: development and initial placement of advertising expensed when first run; other marketing costs expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Business Development
nodes.heading: 1.5.9 Business Development
nodes.start_phrase: Business development expense includes payments to our cobrand partners, corporate client incentive payments earned on achievement of pre-set targets and certain payments to network partners.
nodes.summary:
- Defines contra-revenue as payments to merchants, network partners, and customers, except when goods/services with determinable fair value are received, which are recorded as expenses.
- Explains interest income recognition:
  - Card Member loans: average daily balance method; accrue per account terms until paid or written off, unless on non-accrual.
  - Investment securities: effective interest method (premiums/discounts, fees) until default or when future interest is unlikely.
  - Deposits with banks: recognized as earned from interest-bearing placements.
- Details interest expense recognition as incurred, primarily for funding loans/receivables and liquidity, split into:
  - Deposits: interest on customer/institutional deposits.
  - Debt: interest on long-term debt and short-term borrowings, including realized effects of interest rate hedging derivatives.
- Outlines Card Member rewards accounting:
  - Expense recognized when rewards are earned through spending.
  - Liabilities recorded for expected redemptions and point costs (Membership Rewards, cash back).
  - Cobrand: liability based on rewards earned; payments made to partners, who deliver rewards; liabilities vary with enrollment, attrition, earn/redemption volumes and costs; changes flow through rewards expense.
- Describes business development expenses: payments to cobrand partners, client incentives tied to targets, and certain network partner payments, generally expensed as incurred.
- Notes Card Member services expenses for value-added benefits/services, expensed as incurred.
- States marketing costs: advertising development and initial placement expensed when first run; other marketing expenses expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Card Member Services
nodes.heading: 1.5.10 Card Member Services
nodes.start_phrase: Card Member services expense represents costs incurred in providing our Card Members with various value-added benefits and services, which are generally expensed as incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Defines contra-revenue: payments to merchants, network partners, and customers reduce revenue unless specific, measurable goods/services are received, in which case they are expensed.
- Details interest income recognition:
  - Card Member loans: accrued using the average daily balance method until paid or written off, unless on non-accrual.
  - Investment securities: recognized via the effective interest method, with recognition suspended upon default or likely missed payments.
  - Bank deposits and other interest-bearing accounts: recognized as earned.
- Explains interest expense: recognized as incurred, primarily for funding Card Member loans/receivables, corporate purposes, and liquidity; categorized into deposits and debt, including realized hedge impacts on long-term debt.
- Outlines Card Member rewards accounting:
  - Expense recognized as rewards are earned through spending.
  - Liabilities recorded for expected redemptions and costs for Membership Rewards and cash back.
  - For cobrand programs, liabilities based on rewards earned on spend and payments to partners; partners deliver rewards under their own programs.
  - Changes in liabilities flow through rewards expense in the income statement.
- Business development: includes payments to cobrand partners, corporate client incentives tied to targets, and certain network partner payments; generally expensed as incurred.
- Card Member services: costs for value-added benefits and services; expensed as incurred.
- Marketing: costs for developing and initially placing advertising expensed when first run; other marketing costs expensed as incurred.

nodes.title: Marketing
nodes.heading: 1.5.11 Marketing
nodes.start_phrase: Marketing expense includes costs incurred in the development and initial placement of advertising, which are expensed in the period in which the advertising first takes place.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines revenue and expense recognition policies:
  - Contra-revenue: Payments to merchants, network partners, and customers are recorded as contra-revenue unless goods/services of measurable fair value are received, in which case they’re expensed.
  - Interest income: 
    - Card Member loans accrue interest via the average daily balance method until paid, written off, or in non-accrual.
    - Investment securities use the effective interest method until default or when scheduled payments are unlikely.
    - Bank deposits and other interest-bearing accounts recognize interest as earned.
  - Interest expense: Recognized as incurred, primarily for deposits and debt, including realized impacts of interest rate hedges on long-term debt.
  - Card Member rewards: Expense recognized as rewards are earned through spend; liabilities recorded for expected redemptions and costs (Membership Rewards, cash back) and for cobrand rewards earned, with payments to partners; changes in liabilities flow through rewards expense.
  - Business development: Payments to cobrand partners, corporate client incentives, and certain network partner payments, generally expensed as incurred.
  - Card Member services: Costs of value-added benefits/services, expensed as incurred.
  - Marketing: Advertising expensed when first placed; other marketing costs expensed as incurred.

- Describes balance sheet accounting policies:
  - Cash and cash equivalents: Includes cash, amounts due from banks, interest-bearing balances, resale agreements, restricted cash (e.g., Card Member credit balances, upcoming VIE debt maturities), and highly liquid investments with maturities of 90 days or less.
  - Goodwill: Allocated to reporting units; annual impairment testing (qualitative option with factors like market conditions and performance; quantitative if needed). Quantitative tests use income (DCF with CAPM-based discount rates) and market (multiples) approaches. For 2021 and 2022, fair values exceeded carrying values; quantitative tests tied to operating segment realignment also showed no impairment.
  - Premises and equipment: Carried at cost less accumulated depreciation; construction costs capitalized; straight-line depreciation over:
    - 3–10 years for equipment, furniture, and building improvements
    - 40–50 years for premises
    - Internal-use software capitalized and amortized over ~5 years; reviewed for impairment similar to intangible assets.

nodes.title: BALANCE SHEET
nodes.heading: 1.6 BALANCE SHEET
nodes.start_phrase: Cash and cash equivalents include cash and amounts due from banks, interest-bearing bank balances, including securities purchased under resale agreements, restricted cash, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
nodes.summary:
- Accounting policies for key balance sheet items:
  - Cash and cash equivalents: definition and components (cash, due from banks, interest-bearing balances, securities under resale agreements, other highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less).
  - Restricted cash: primarily relates to Card Member credit balances and upcoming debt maturities of consolidated VIEs.
- Goodwill:
  - Definition and allocation to reporting units (operating segments or one level below) for impairment testing.
  - Annual impairment testing as of June 30, with interim testing upon triggering events; recoverability test of certain long-lived assets performed beforehand.
  - Option for qualitative assessment (reviewing macroeconomic, industry, cost, financial performance, and entity-specific factors) to determine need for quantitative testing.
  - Quantitative assessment methodology: compare reporting unit fair value to carrying amount; recognize impairment if carrying exceeds fair value.
  - Valuation techniques: income approach (DCF using internal forecasts and CAPM-derived cost of equity) and market approach (comparable company multiples).
  - 2021 and 2022 results: qualitative assessments indicated fair values exceeded carrying values; 2022 quantitative tests for units affected by operating segment realignment also showed no impairment (fair values exceeded carrying amounts).
- Premises and equipment:
  - Carried at cost less accumulated depreciation; construction costs capitalized until placed in service.
  - Straight-line depreciation: 3–10 years for equipment, furniture, and building improvements; 40–50 years for premises (based on estimated useful life at acquisition).
  - Internal-use software: certain development/acquisition costs capitalized within premises and equipment; amortized straight-line over generally 5 years; subject to impairment testing consistent with intangible assets.

nodes.title: Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.heading: 1.6.1 Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.start_phrase: Cash and cash equivalents include cash and amounts due from banks, interest-bearing bank balances, including securities purchased under resale agreements, restricted cash, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
nodes.summary:
- Defines components of cash and cash equivalents, including interest-bearing balances, securities purchased under resale agreements, and restricted cash; notes restricted cash relates to Card Member credit balances and upcoming consolidated VIE debt maturities.
- Explains goodwill recognition and allocation to reporting units; outlines annual and interim impairment testing, including optional qualitative assessment and quantitative assessment triggers.
- Details qualitative factors considered (economic, industry, cost, financial performance, and unit-specific events) and quantitative methods comparing carrying amount to fair value.
- Describes valuation techniques for goodwill testing: income approach (discounted cash flows using internal forecasts and CAPM-based cost of equity) and market approach (peer market multiples).
- Discloses results: for years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021, qualitative tests indicated fair values exceeded carrying values; in 2022, quantitative tests for units affected by operating segment realignment also showed fair values exceeded carrying values (no impairment).
- Covers premises and equipment accounting: carried at cost less accumulated depreciation; capitalization of construction costs; straight-line depreciation (3–10 years for equipment/furniture/building improvements; 40–50 years for premises).
- Addresses internal-use software: capitalization of certain acquisition/development costs within premises and equipment; amortized straight-line over generally 5 years; impairment reviewed using the intangible asset methodology.

nodes.title: Goodwill
nodes.heading: 1.6.2 Goodwill
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill represents the excess of the acquisition cost of an acquired business over the fair value of assets acquired and liabilities assumed.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Balance sheet accounting policies covering cash and cash equivalents, goodwill, and premises and equipment (including internal‑use software).
- Cash and cash equivalents: Include cash, amounts due from banks, interest-bearing bank balances, securities purchased under resale agreements, restricted cash, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less. Restricted cash mainly relates to Card Member credit balances and upcoming debt maturities of consolidated VIEs.
- Goodwill: Defined as excess purchase price over fair value of net assets in acquisitions; allocated to reporting units (operating segments or components). Impairment testing performed annually as of June 30 or upon triggering events, with an initial qualitative option followed by a quantitative test if needed. Quantitative valuation uses income (DCF with internal forecasts, CAPM-based cost of equity) and market approaches (public company multiples). Preceded by recoverability tests for certain long-lived assets. For 2022 and 2021, assessments indicated fair values exceeded carrying values; a quantitative test tied to operating segment realignment also showed no impairment (see Note 24).
- Premises and equipment: Recorded at cost less accumulated depreciation; construction costs capitalized; straight-line depreciation. Useful lives: 3–10 years for equipment, furniture, and building improvements; 40–50 years for premises (based on useful life at acquisition).
- Internal-use software: Certain acquisition/development costs capitalized within premises and equipment; amortized straight-line over generally 5 years; impairment assessed using the methodology applied to intangible assets.

nodes.title: Premises and Equipment
nodes.heading: 1.6.3 Premises and Equipment
nodes.start_phrase: Premises and equipment, including leasehold improvements, are carried at cost less accumulated depreciation.
nodes.summary:
- Covers balance sheet accounting policies and related notes.
- Cash and cash equivalents: includes cash, due from banks, interest-bearing balances, securities purchased under resale agreements, restricted cash, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less; restricted cash relates to Card Member credit balances and upcoming maturities of consolidated VIE debt.
- Goodwill: allocated to reporting units; annual impairment testing as of June 30 or upon triggering events; option for qualitative or quantitative assessment. Qualitative factors include macroeconomic, industry, cost, performance, and unit-specific considerations. Quantitative assessment compares carrying value to fair value using income (discounted cash flows with CAPM-based cost of equity) and market (comparable company multiples) approaches. For 2022 and 2021, fair values exceeded carrying values; quantitative tests due to operating segment realignment also supported no impairment (see Note 24).
- Premises and equipment: carried at cost less accumulated depreciation. Useful lives—equipment/furniture/building improvements: 3–10 years; premises: 40–50 years. Capitalization and amortization of internal-use software (generally 5 years) with impairment review aligned to intangible asset methodology. Leasehold improvements depreciated over the shorter of lease term or economic life (5–10 years); recognition of lease restoration obligations and amortization of related assets over the lease term.
- Leases: operating leases for facilities/equipment recognized as right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for terms >12 months; non-lease components not separated. Lease liabilities measured at present value of fixed payments using the incremental borrowing rate at commencement or modification. Operating lease expense recognized straight-line; variable payments expensed as incurred.
- Other significant accounting policies cross-referenced to notes: Loans and Card Member Receivables (Note 2), Reserves for Credit Losses (Note 3), Investment Securities (Note 4), Asset Securitizations (Note 5), Contingencies and Commitments (Note 12), Derivatives and Hedging Activities (Note 13), Fair Values (Note 14), Guarantees (Note 15), Income Taxes (Note 20).
- Classification: certain prior-period amounts reclassified to conform to current period presentation.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: 1.6.4 Leases
nodes.start_phrase: We have operating leases worldwide for facilities and equipment, which, for those leases with terms greater than 12 months, are recorded as lease-related assets and liabilities.
nodes.summary:
- Leasehold improvements: depreciated on a straight-line basis over the lesser of the remaining lease term or the asset’s economic life (typically 5–10 years). Lease restoration obligations are recorded at fair value when incurred, with related assets amortized over the lease term.
- Lease accounting: operating leases for facilities and equipment (terms >12 months) are recognized as right-of-use assets and corresponding lease liabilities. The company does not separate lease and non-lease components. Right-of-use assets are measured at lease commencement equal to lease liabilities, adjusted for prepaid amounts, initial direct costs, and incentives. Lease liabilities are measured at the present value of fixed payments using the incremental borrowing rate at commencement or modification. Operating lease expense is recognized straight-line; variable lease payments are expensed as incurred.
- Other significant accounting policies: references to notes covering Loans and Card Member Receivables (Note 2), Reserves for Credit Losses (Note 3), Investment Securities (Note 4), Asset Securitizations (Note 5), Contingencies and Commitments (Note 12), Derivatives and Hedging Activities (Note 13), Fair Values (Note 14), Guarantees (Note 15), and Income Taxes (Note 20).
- Classification: certain prior period amounts were reclassified to conform to the current period presentation.

nodes.title: OTHER SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.heading: 1.7 OTHER SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
nodes.start_phrase: The following table identifies our other significant accounting policies, along with the related Note.
nodes.summary:
- Describes accounting for leasehold improvements: depreciated on a straight-line basis over the lesser of the remaining lease term or the asset’s economic life (generally 5–10 years). Restoration obligations are recognized at fair value when incurred, with related restoration assets amortized over the lease term.
- Explains lease accounting for operating leases: right-of-use assets and lease liabilities are recorded for leases over 12 months; lease and non-lease components are not separated. Right-of-use assets are measured at lease commencement equal to the lease liability, adjusted for prepaid amounts, initial direct costs, and incentives. Lease liabilities are the present value of fixed payments discounted using the incremental borrowing rate at commencement or upon modification. Operating lease expense is recognized on a straight-line basis; variable payments are expensed as incurred.
- Lists other significant accounting policies with cross-references to related notes, including loans and card member receivables, reserves for credit losses, investment securities, asset securitizations, legal contingencies, derivatives and hedging, fair value measurements, guarantees, and income taxes.
- Notes that certain prior-period amounts were reclassified to conform to the current period presentation.

nodes.title: CLASSIFICATION OF VARIOUS ITEMS
nodes.heading: 1.8 CLASSIFICATION OF VARIOUS ITEMS
nodes.start_phrase: Certain reclassifications of prior period amounts have been made to conform to the current period presentation.
nodes.summary:
- Leasehold improvements: depreciated straight-line over the shorter of lease term or asset life (typically 5–10 years); recognize lease restoration obligations at fair value and amortize related assets over the lease term.
- Lease accounting: operating leases for facilities/equipment recognized as right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for terms >12 months; do not separate lease and non-lease components; ROU assets measured at commencement equal to lease liabilities adjusted for prepaids, initial direct costs, and incentives; lease liabilities measured at present value of fixed payments using the incremental borrowing rate; operating lease expense recognized straight-line; variable lease payments expensed as incurred.
- Other significant accounting policies and related notes: Loans and Card Member Receivables (Note 2), Reserves for Credit Losses (Note 3), Investment Securities (Note 4), Asset Securitizations (Note 5), Legal Contingencies (Note 12), Derivatives and Hedging Activities (Note 13), Fair Value Measurements (Note 14), Guarantees (Note 15), Income Taxes (Note 20).
- Classification: certain prior-period amounts reclassified to conform to current presentation.
- Recently issued/adopted standards: 2022 FASB guidance eliminating TDR accounting (for CECL adopters), creating a single loan modification model and enhanced disclosures; adopted prospectively beginning Q1 2023 with no material impact; CECL adopted January 1, 2020 via modified retrospective method, increasing credit loss reserves and reducing opening retained earnings (see Note 3).

nodes.title: RECENTLY ISSUED AND ADOPTED ACCOUNTING STANDARDS
nodes.heading: 1.9 RECENTLY ISSUED AND ADOPTED ACCOUNTING STANDARDS
nodes.start_phrase: In March 2022, the Financial Accounting Standards Board issued new accounting guidance on troubled debt restructuring (TDR) and write-offs, effective January 1, 2023, with early adoption permitted.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of recently issued and adopted accounting standards:
  - FASB’s March 2022 guidance eliminates TDR accounting for CECL adopters, creates a single loan modification model, and enhances disclosures for modifications and write-offs.
  - Effective January 1, 2023; adoption will be prospective beginning Q1 2023 and is not expected to be material to the Consolidated Financial Statements.
  - CECL was adopted on January 1, 2020 via a modified retrospective approach, increasing credit loss reserves with an offset to opening retained earnings; Note 3 covers reserve estimation.

- Note 2 — Loans and Card Member Receivables:
  - Describes Card Member loans (revolve-eligible transactions, finance charges, minimum payments, variable terms) and policy to cease interest accrual upon write-off; loans presented net of credit loss reserves, including accrued interest/fees.
  - Describes Other loans (non-card financing to consumers/commercials with fixed terms and monthly payments) presented net of credit loss reserves.

- Portfolio balances as of December 31:
  - 2022 Card Member loans: $107.964B (Consumer $84.964B; Small Business $22.947B; Corporate $0.053B); reserves $3.747B; net $104.217B.
  - 2021 Card Member loans: $88.562B (Consumer $70.467B; Small Business $18.040B; Corporate $0.055B); reserves $3.305B; net $85.257B.
  - Other loans, net: $5.357B (2022) vs. $2.859B (2021); reserves on Other loans: $59M (2022) vs. $52M (2021).
  - Footnotes: Approximately $28.5B (2022) and $26.6B (2021) of gross Card Member loans support obligations of a consolidated VIE; Other loans include PPP balances of $7M (2022) and $36M (2021).

nodes.title: LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
nodes.heading: NOTE 2 LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
nodes.start_phrase: Our lending and charge payment card products that we offer to consumer, small business and corporate customers result in the generation of Card Member loans and Card Member receivables.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 2 — Loans and Card Member Receivables for consumer, small business, and corporate customers, plus non-card financing (“Other loans”).
- Card Member loans: Recognized at point-of-sale; include revolve-eligible balances, finance charges, and fees. Card Members must make minimum payments; revolving balances accrue finance charges. Terms (limits, rates, fees, payment structures) can change based on new information and regulations. Loans are presented net of credit loss reserves and include principal, accrued interest, and fees. Interest accrual stops upon write-off; reserves established for uncollectible interest.
- Other loans: Non-card financing recorded when credit is extended; generally fixed terms with monthly repayment; governed by separate agreements. Presented net of credit loss reserves; include principal, accrued interest, and fees.
- Balances as of December 31:
  - 2022 Card Member loans (gross): Consumer $84.964b; Small Business $22.947b; Corporate $0.053b; Total $107.964b. Reserves $3.747b; Net $104.217b.
  - 2021 Card Member loans (gross): Consumer $70.467b; Small Business $18.040b; Corporate $0.055b; Total $88.562b. Reserves $3.305b; Net $85.257b.
  - Other loans, net: $5.357b (2022) vs. $2.859b (2021).
- Footnotes:
  - Approximately $28.5b (2022) and $26.6b (2021) of gross Card Member loans are available to settle obligations of a consolidated VIE.
  - Other loans include non-card financing and SBA PPP loans, with $7m (2022) and $36m (2021) of PPP loans outstanding.
  - Other loans are presented net of reserves for credit losses of $59m (2022) and $52m (2021).
- Cross-reference: Credit loss reserves referenced to Note 3.

nodes.title: LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES - Introduction
nodes.source_heading: NOTE 2 LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
nodes.heading: NOTE 2 LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
nodes.start_phrase: Our lending and charge payment card products that we offer to consumer, small business and corporate customers result in the generation of Card Member loans and Card Member receivables.
nodes.summary:
LOANS AND CARD MEMBER RECEIVABLES
Our lending and charge payment card products that we offer to consumer, small business and corporate customers result in the generation of Card Member
loans and Card Member receivables. We also extend credit to customers through non-card financing products, resulting in Other loans.

nodes.title: CARD MEMBER AND OTHER LOANS
nodes.heading: 2.1 CARD MEMBER AND OTHER LOANS
nodes.start_phrase: Card Member loans are generally recorded at the time a Card Member enters into a point-of-sale transaction with a merchant and represent revolve-eligible transactions on our card products, as well as any finance charges and associated card-related fees.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 2 – Loans and Card Member Receivables, covering card-related lending and charge products, and non‑card financing.
- Card Member loans: Recognized at point of sale for revolve‑eligible transactions, including finance charges and fees. Card Members make minimum payments; revolving balances incur finance charges. - Focus: Credit quality indicators, impaired loans/receivables, and Troubled Debt Restructurings (TDRs) for card member loans and receivables, with data and disclosures for years ended December 31, 2022, 2021, and 2020.

- Credit quality indicators (2022 vs. 2021):

- Definitions and impairment approach:
  - Impaired assets include loans 90+ days past due still accruing, non-accrual loans, and TDRs.
  - TDRs arise from customer financial relief programs aimed at minimizing losses and improving collectability.
  - Typical modifications: temporary interest rate reductions (can be to 0%, which are then non-accrual in TDR disclosures), fixed payment plans up to 60 months, suspension of delinquency fees; purchasing ability is limited/canceled/suspended during programs.
  - Accounts may revert to original terms upon program exit (successful completion or default).
  - Reserves for TDRs measured individually via discounted cash flow; changes flow through provision for credit losses.

- Impaired balances and reserves (as of year-end):
  - 2022 total impaired balance $4.3B; TDR reserve $504M.
  - 2021 total impaired balance $3.4B; TDR reserve $596M.
  - 2020 total impaired balance $3.9B; TDR reserve $1.35B.
  - Breakdowns provided across Consumer/Small Business card loans, Consumer/Small Business/Corporate receivables, and Other Loans (non-card financing).
  - Additional disclosures identify portions of TDRs that are also 90+ days past due or non-accrual, and distinguish “In Program” vs. “Out of Program” TDRs (completed vs. non-compliant accounts).

- Policy notes:
  - Interest generally accrued through write-off at ~180 days past due (with reserves for uncollectible interest).
  - Corporate receivable write-off rate on principal-only not available due to system constraints.
  - Reference to Note 3 for additional qualitative credit risk indicators.

- TDR activity during the year (modifications executed):
  - 2022: 180K accounts; $1.91B balances modified. Card loans average interest rate reduction 14 percentage points; no term extensions. Receivables have no rate reductions (non-interest bearing) with ~20-month average term extensions. Other loans: ~2 pp rate reduction, ~17-month extensions.
  - 2021: 137K accounts; $1.24B modified; similar terms (card loans ~13 pp rate cuts, no extensions; receivables ~18-month extensions).
  - 2020: 328K accounts; $3.89B modified; larger pandemic-era relief (card loans ~14 pp cuts; receivables ~19-month extensions; other loans ~3 pp cuts, ~16-month extensions).

  - Uses Probability of Default (PD), Exposure at Default (EAD), and recovery models; EAD reflects revolving behavior and expected repayments; recovery models consider timing since default and macroeconomic conditions.

nodes.title: RESERVES FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.heading: NOTE 3 RESERVES FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.start_phrase: Reserves for credit losses represent our best estimate of the expected credit losses in our outstanding portfolio of Card Member loans and receivables as of the balance sheet date.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Note on Reserves for Credit Losses under CECL for Card Member loans and receivables.
- Methodology:
  - CECL estimates lifetime expected credit losses using historical loss experience plus current and forward-looking conditions over a reasonable and supportable (R&S) period of about three years, then reverts to long-term average loss rates.
  - Key models: Probability of Default (PD), Exposure at Default (EAD), and Recovery models projected monthly over the R&S period.
  - EAD reflects expected future spending and payment/revolve behavior; recovery models consider time since default and macro conditions.
  - Expected recoveries of previously written-off accounts are estimated and can exceed expected losses.
- Macroeconomic scenarios:
  - Multiple third-party scenarios (e.g., unemployment, real GDP) are incorporated; management applies judgmental weights each period.
  - A table provides ranges of U.S. unemployment and real GDP assumptions used as of Dec 31, 2022 and 2021 for near-term and subsequent quarters.
- Qualitative adjustments:
  - Management may overlay qualitative reserves to address model limitations and emerging risks (external conditions, portfolio trends, concentrations, delinquency, risk actions).
- Measurement granularity and special cases:
  - Assets evaluated at pooled levels with similar risk characteristics (spend/remittance behavior, credit scores, delinquency, tenure, etc.).
  - Credit losses on accrued interest are recognized within reserves and provisions, not via interest income reversal.
  - Troubled debt restructurings (TDRs) are modeled individually using discounted cash flows.
- Charge-off policies:
  - Write-offs generally no later than 180 days past due for pay-in-full/revolving loans and 120 days for term loans; immediate write-off upon bankruptcy/death notification.
- Reserve rollforward and drivers:
  - 2022: Card Member loans reserve increased due to higher loans outstanding, higher delinquencies, and macro forecast changes, partly offset by releasing COVID-19-related reserves.
  - 2021: Reserve decreased on improved portfolio quality and macro outlook (notably unemployment), partly offset by loan growth.
  - Rollforward (millions):
    - 2022: Begin $3,305; Provisions $1,514; Net write-offs principal $(837), interest/fees $(229); Other $(6); End $3,747.
    - 2021: Begin $5,344; Provisions $(1,155); Net write-offs principal $(672), interest/fees $(207); Other $(5); End $3,305.
    - 2020: Begin $4,027; Provisions $3,453; Net write-offs principal $(1,795), interest/fees $(375); Other $34; End $5,344.
  - Notes: Principal write-offs shown net of recoveries ($539m in 2022; $657m in 2021; $568m in 2020). Includes net TDR (write-offs)/recoveries. Other mainly FX translation adjustments.

nodes.title: RESERVES FOR CREDIT LOSSES - Introduction
nodes.heading: NOTE 3 RESERVES FOR CREDIT LOSSES
nodes.start_phrase: Reserves for credit losses represent our best estimate of the expected credit losses in our outstanding portfolio of Card Member loans and receivables as of the balance sheet date.
nodes.summary: Overview of the company’s CECL-based methodology for reserves on Card Member loans and receivables, estimating lifetime expected credit losses over a roughly three-year reasonable and supportable (R&S) period using PD, EAD, and recovery models with immediate reversion to long-term average loss rates thereafter. Models incorporate third‑party macroeconomic scenarios (weighted by management) featuring key variables such as U.S. unemployment and real GDP, and also estimate recoveries on previously written‑off accounts. Qualitative reserves may adjust quantitative outputs for model limitations and factors like external conditions, emerging trends, portfolio concentrations, delinquency levels, and management actions. Losses are evaluated at granular/pooled levels by shared risk characteristics (e.g., spend/remittance behavior, credit bureau scores, delinquency, tenure); accrued interest is included in reserves and provision lines. Troubled debt restructurings are measured individually using discounted cash flow models. Write‑off policies generally occur no later than 180 days past due for pay‑in‑full or revolving loans and 120 days for term loans, with bankruptcy/deceased accounts written off upon notification. A table presents ranges of U.S. unemployment and real GDP (QoQ SAAR) assumptions used in scenarios for Q4 2022, Q1 2023, Q4 2023, and Q4 2024 as of December 31, 2022 and 2021.

- Note 5 — Asset Securitizations:

Long‑term debt (original maturities of one year or more) totaled $42.57 billion at a 3.42% year‑end rate in 2022 versus $38.68 billion at 2.22% in 2021, including issuances by the Parent (fixed, floating, and fixed‑to‑floating senior and subordinated notes with maturities 2023–2042), American Express Credit Corporation (reduced fixed‑rate notes, no floating‑rate notes outstanding), Lending Trust (higher fixed‑rate senior notes, lower floating‑rate senior notes, minimal subordinated notes), Charge Trust (no 2022 conduit borrowings vs. $2.0 billion in 2021), and other finance leases and floating‑rate borrowings; unamortized underwriting fees reduced the total. The tables present both stated interest rates and, where applicable, “interest rate with swaps” for hedged tranches; floating‑rate figures are weighted by outstanding balances and current rates. Footnotes explain that outstanding balances include unamortized discounts, foreign currency effects, and fair value hedge adjustments on swapped fixed‑rate notes (with a cross‑reference to the fair value hedge accounting note). Overall, 2022 reflects higher parent‑level fixed‑rate issuance (including new 2033 fixed‑to‑floating senior and subordinated notes), growth in Lending Trust fixed‑rate funding, runoff of Credit Corporation and Charge Trust borrowings, and a higher overall cost of debt year over year.

- Derivatives and Hedging Activities
  - Purpose and scope: Derivatives used to manage market risk (not for trading), recorded at fair value; risks include interest rate risk and foreign exchange risk.
  - Risk governance: Central monitoring under an Asset/Liability Management Policy with limits and escalation triggers.
  - Interest rate risk management: Arises from funding receivables and fixed-rate loans with variable-rate borrowings and shifts in benchmark relationships; managed via mix of variable- vs fixed-rate debt/deposits and use of interest rate swaps to convert exposures.
  - Foreign exchange risk management: Exposures from non-billing currency spend, cross-currency funding, investments in foreign subsidiaries and non-USD revenues/expenses; managed with spot transactions and FX forwards where economical.
  - Counterparty credit risk: Evaluated via current and potential future exposure; counterparties must be investment grade and pre-approved; exposures centrally monitored.

nodes.title: DERIVATIVES AND HEDGING ACTIVITIES
nodes.heading: NOTE 13 DERIVATIVES AND HEDGING ACTIVITIES
nodes.start_phrase: We use derivative financial instruments to manage exposures to various market risks.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: The note explains the company’s use of derivative financial instruments—carried at fair value and not used for trading—to manage market risks, primarily interest rate and foreign exchange (FX) risk. Exposures largely arise as by-products of delivering products and services.
- Market risk overview and governance:
  - Key risks: interest rate risk (mismatch between asset and liability rates and benchmark relationships) and FX risk (non-USD transactions, funding, investments, and earnings).
  - Governance: centralized monitoring under the Asset/Liability Management Policy with limits and escalation triggers.
- Interest rate risk management:
  - Managed by adjusting the mix of variable-/short-term vs fixed-rate funding for receivables and fixed-rate loans.
  - Use of interest rate swaps to convert fixed-rate debt to floating or vice versa; mix can change with business volumes and mix.
- Foreign exchange risk management:
  - FX exposures from: (1) Card Member spend in non-billing currencies, (2) cross-currency funding, (3) cross-currency investing (e.g., equity in foreign subs), (4) non-USD revenues/expenses.
  - Managed via spot transactions and, when economical, derivatives such as FX forwards.
- Counterparty credit risk and collateral:
  - Counterparties must be pre-approved and investment grade; exposures (current and potential future) are centrally monitored.
  - Master netting agreements in place; credit support agreements require collateral posting when thresholds are exceeded.
  - Centrally cleared derivatives are fully collateralized; downgrade clauses allow counterparties to terminate if the company falls below investment grade.
  - As of Dec 31, 2022: no material net liability position, no material single-counterparty exposure, and no credit risk adjustment required (same in 2021).
- Balance sheet presentation and netting:
  - Derivatives recorded at fair value; assets and liabilities with the same counterparty presented net when appropriate.
  - Cash collateral netting applied for bilateral interest rate and certain FX contracts; variation margin on cleared derivatives treated as settlement, not collateral.
  - Initial margin on cleared swaps recorded in Other assets and not netted.
- Fair value amounts (2022 vs 2021):
  - Hedging derivatives include interest rate fair value hedges and FX net investment hedges.
  - Non-designated derivatives primarily FX and other.
  - The note provides gross and net derivative asset/liability amounts, including effects of derivative and cash collateral netting.
- Hedge accounting framework:
  - Hedges are documented and designated at inception; effectiveness assessed at inception and quarterly (typically via regression).
  - Hedge accounting discontinued if not highly effective.
- Fair value hedges—interest rate contracts:
  - Fixed-rate long-term debt designated in fair value hedges using interest rate swaps to economically convert to floating.
  - $8.1 billion (2022) and $12.9 billion (2021) of fixed-rate debt in such hedging relationships.
  - Gains/losses on swaps generally offset changes in the hedged debt attributable to the hedged risk; offsets may be imperfect due to credit spread components not reflected in swap fair value.
- Cross-reference: Fair value measurement methodologies for derivatives are described in Note 14.

nodes.title: DERIVATIVES AND HEDGING ACTIVITIES - Introduction
nodes.heading: NOTE 13 DERIVATIVES AND HEDGING ACTIVITIES
nodes.start_phrase: We use derivative financial instruments to manage exposures to various market risks.
nodes.summary: Overview of the company’s derivatives and hedging program used solely for risk management, not trading, covering interest rate and foreign exchange exposures monitored under the Asset/Liability Management Policy. Interest rate risk arises from funding Card Member receivables and fixed-rate loans with variable-rate borrowings and benchmark shifts (Prime, SOFR, OIS); it is managed via funding mix and interest rate swaps that convert fixed-to-variable or variable-to-fixed. Foreign exchange risk stems from non-billing-currency spend, cross-currency funding and investing (including net investments in foreign subs), and FX-denominated revenues/expenses; it is managed with spot transactions and FX forwards. Counterparty credit risk is controlled through investment-grade, pre-approved counterparties, central monitoring, master netting and credit support agreements with collateral posting, and full collateralization for centrally cleared trades; some contracts permit termination upon a downgrade below investment grade. As of December 31, 2022 and 2021, no credit risk adjustment was required; 2022 positions were not in a material net liability and there was no material exposure to any single counterparty. Derivatives are carried at fair value; hedge designations include fair value hedges (interest rate) and net investment hedges (FX). Fair value summary (excluding interest accruals): at 12/31/2022, gross assets $521m and liabilities $801m; after netting and cash collateral, net assets $253m and net liabilities $332m (components include fair value hedge interest rate contracts: $0 assets, $211m liabilities; net investment hedge FX: $350m assets, $251m liabilities; non-designated FX/other: $171m assets, $339m liabilities). At 12/31/2021, gross assets $590m and liabilities $139m; net assets $293m and net liabilities $42m; initial margin posted on centrally cleared interest rate swaps was $8m (2022) and $11m (2021), recorded in Other assets and not netted, and variation margin on cleared derivatives is treated as settlement.

nodes.heading: 13.1 DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS THAT QUALIFY FOR HEDGE ACCOUNTING

  - Non-designated derivatives (primarily foreign exchange and other).

  - Used to hedge changes in the fair value of assets/liabilities attributable to specific risks.

nodes.title: DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS THAT QUALIFY FOR HEDGE ACCOUNTING - Introduction
nodes.source_title: DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS THAT QUALIFY FOR HEDGE ACCOUNTING
nodes.source_heading: DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS THAT QUALIFY FOR HEDGE ACCOUNTING
nodes.heading: 13.1 DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS THAT QUALIFY FOR HEDGE ACCOUNTING
nodes.start_phrase: Derivatives executed for hedge accounting purposes are documented and designated as such when we enter into the contracts.
nodes.summary:
DERIVATIVE FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS THAT QUALIFY FOR HEDGE ACCOUNTING
Derivatives executed for hedge accounting purposes are documented and designated as such when we enter into the contracts. In accordance with our risk
management policies, we structure our hedges with terms similar to those of the item being hedged. We formally assess, at inception of the hedge accounting
relationship and on a quarterly basis, whether derivatives designated as hedges are highly effective in offsetting the fair value or cash flows of the hedged
items. These assessments usually are made through the application of a regression analysis method. If it is determined that a derivative is not highly effective as
a hedge, we will discontinue the application of hedge accounting.

nodes.title: FAIR VALUES
nodes.heading: NOTE 14 FAIR VALUES
nodes.start_phrase: Fair value is defined as the price that would be required to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, based on the principal or, in the absence of a principal, most advantageous market for the specific asset or liability.
nodes.summary:
- Note 14 outlines the company’s fair value measurements under GAAP, defining fair value as the exit price in the principal (or most advantageous) market at the measurement date.
- It explains the three-level GAAP fair value hierarchy:
  - Level 1: quoted prices for identical items in active markets.
  - Level 2: observable inputs other than Level 1 (e.g., quoted prices for similar items, inactive markets, or market-corroborated inputs).
  - Level 3: unobservable inputs reflecting the company’s own assumptions.
- The company reviews market conditions and hierarchy classifications at least quarterly; there were no Level 3 transfers in 2022 or 2021.
- Recurring fair value measurements as of December 31:
  - 2022 assets: $5,099 million (Level 1: $40m, Level 2: $4,985m, Level 3: $74m). Key categories:
    - Equity securities: $41m (primarily Level 1).

    - Derivative assets (gross): $521m (mostly Level 2; $27m Level 3).
  - 2022 liabilities: $801 million, all derivative liabilities (gross), entirely Level 2.
  - 2021 assets: $3,181 million (Level 1: $78m, Level 2: $3,071m, Level 3: $32m).
  - 2021 liabilities: $139 million, all Level 2 derivative liabilities (gross).
- Level 3 amounts include an embedded derivative valued by an independent third party using a Monte Carlo simulation in a risk-neutral framework based on implied volatility, with management applying judgment to the valuation.
- Cross-references: Note 4 for investment securities details and Note 13 for derivatives and the embedded derivative.

nodes.title: FAIR VALUES - Introduction
nodes.heading: NOTE 14 FAIR VALUES
nodes.start_phrase: Fair value is defined as the price that would be required to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, based on the principal or, in the absence of a principal, most advantageous market for the specific asset or liability.
nodes.summary: Defines fair value as the exit price in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, determined using the principal or most advantageous market, and summarizes the GAAP three-level fair value hierarchy: Level 1 (unadjusted quoted prices for identical items in active markets), Level 2 (other observable inputs including quotes for similar items, quotes in inactive markets, and inputs corroborated by market data), and Level 3 (unobservable inputs reflecting the company’s assumptions about market participant inputs, e.g., timing and amounts of expected cash flows). Notes the company monitors market conditions and evaluates hierarchy classifications at least quarterly, and reports no Level 3 transfers for the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021.

  - Liabilities primarily Level 2 derivatives.

- Describes valuation techniques for investment securities:
  - Level 1: quoted prices for identical securities.
  - Level 2: third-party pricing services using observable inputs (benchmark yields/prices, credit spreads, prepayment speeds, reported trades, broker quotes); annual reaffirmation of methods and price corroboration; no pricing adjustments by services or by the company.

  - Level 3 embedded derivative (seller earnout shares tied to Global Business Travel Group’s business combination with Apollo Strategic Growth Capital) valued by an independent third party using a Monte Carlo simulation with key inputs (term, initial stock price, expected volatility, risk-neutral rate, dividend yield), reviewed by management.

nodes.title: VALUATION TECHNIQUES USED IN THE FAIR VALUE MEASUREMENT OF FINANCIAL ASSETS AND FINANCIAL LIABILITIES CARRIED AT FAIR VALUE
nodes.heading: 14.2 VALUATION TECHNIQUES USED IN THE FAIR VALUE MEASUREMENT OF FINANCIAL ASSETS AND FINANCIAL LIABILITIES CARRIED AT FAIR VALUE
nodes.start_phrase: For the financial assets and liabilities measured at fair value on a recurring basis (categorized in the valuation hierarchy table above), we apply the following valuation techniques:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Outlines how the company measures fair value for financial assets and liabilities, distinguishing recurring fair value measurements (Levels 1–3) from instruments measured at amortized cost, with governance around pricing validation.

- Investment securities:
  - Level 1: Quoted prices for identical securities in active markets.
  - Level 2: Prices from external pricing services using observable inputs (e.g., benchmark yields/prices, credit spreads, prepayment speeds, reported trades, broker quotes). No adjustments made by pricing services or the company; prices are corroborated against alternative sources and methods are reaffirmed at least annually.
  - Level 3: Debt securities issued by Community Development Financial Institutions measured at carrying value unless internal credit analysis indicates cash flow shortfalls.

- Derivative financial instruments:
  - Level 2: Valued via third-party models with observable inputs; methods applied consistently and reviewed at least annually with quarterly validation.
    - Interest rate swaps: Discounted cash flow using notional, fixed/floating rates, tenor, and currency-consistent discount rates.
    - FX forwards: Discounted cash flow using notional, maturity, contract rate, forward curves, and currency-consistent discount rates.
  - Level 3: Embedded derivative (seller earnout shares related to Global Business Travel Group transaction) valued by an independent party using Monte Carlo simulation with key inputs (term, initial stock price, expected volatility, risk-free rate, dividend yield), reviewed by management.
  - Credit valuation adjustments: Applied to reflect counterparty and own credit risk using observable forecasted default rates.

- Financial assets and liabilities carried at other than fair value (amortized cost):
  - Presents carrying amounts and estimated fair values as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, including hierarchy levels where applicable.
  - 2022 highlights (billions): Cash and cash equivalents $34 (fair value ≈ carrying; Levels 1–2), Other financial assets $60 (Level 2), Card Member and Other loans $110 carrying/$113 fair (Level 3), Financial liabilities approximating fair value $123 (Level 2), Certificates of deposit $16 (Level 2), Long-term debt $43 carrying/$42 fair (Level 2).
  - 2021 highlights (billions): Cash and cash equivalents $22, Other financial assets $56, Card Member and Other loans $88/$91, Financial liabilities approximating fair value $105, Certificates of deposit $5, Long-term debt $39/$40.

nodes.title: VALUATION TECHNIQUES USED IN THE FAIR VALUE MEASUREMENT OF FINANCIAL ASSETS AND FINANCIAL LIABILITIES CARRIED AT OTHER THAN FAIR VALUE
nodes.heading: 14.4 VALUATION TECHNIQUES USED IN THE FAIR VALUE MEASUREMENT OF FINANCIAL ASSETS AND FINANCIAL LIABILITIES CARRIED AT OTHER THAN FAIR VALUE
nodes.start_phrase: For the financial assets and liabilities that are not required to be carried at fair value on a recurring basis (categorized in the valuation hierarchy table), we apply the following valuation techniques to measure fair value:
nodes.summary: The excerpt details the company’s valuation approaches for financial assets and liabilities not carried at fair value on a recurring basis. It specifies which items’ carrying amounts approximate fair value—such as cash and cash equivalents, Card Member receivables, accrued interest, certain other assets, accrued interest on liabilities, non-CD customer deposits, Travelers Cheques and other prepaid products, accounts payable, short-term borrowings, and certain other liabilities—primarily due to short duration, no defined maturity, or market-based rates. For assets carried at other than fair value, Card Member and Other loans are recorded at historical cost less reserves, with fair value estimated via a discounted cash flow model using projected income, discount rates, and forecasted write-offs, excluding any value from future receivables generation. For liabilities carried at other than fair value, Certificates of Deposit are valued using discounted cash flows at current market rates for comparable CDs. Long-term debt is recorded at historical cost with adjustments for unamortized discounts/fees, foreign exchange on non-USD debt, and hedge accounting effects; fair value is based on quoted offer prices when available or discounted cash flows using market rates for similar term and credit risk, incorporating company-specific credit spreads informed by CDS spreads, the company’s bond yields, and current offered rates. The section also notes nonrecurring fair value measurements for assets when impairment occurs or when observable price changes arise for equity investments without readily determinable fair values.

nodes.title: REGULATORY MATTERS AND CAPITAL ADEQUACY
nodes.heading: NOTE 22 REGULATORY MATTERS AND CAPITAL ADEQUACY
nodes.start_phrase: We are supervised and regulated by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the Federal Reserve) and are subject to the Federal Reserve’s requirements for risk-based capital and leverage ratios.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 22—Regulatory matters, capital adequacy, and restricted net assets.
- Oversight: American Express Company is regulated by the Federal Reserve; its U.S. bank subsidiary, American Express National Bank (AENB), by the OCC.
- Capital framework: Subject to Basel III risk-based and leverage requirements, including minimum CET1, Tier 1, Total capital ratios to risk-weighted assets, and a Tier 1 leverage ratio. Failure to meet minimums could trigger regulatory actions.
- Compliance status: As of December 31, 2022 and 2021, both the Company and AENB met all requirements and exceeded well-capitalized standards.
- Reported capital metrics:
  - 2022—Company: CET1 $20.03B; Tier 1 $21.63B; Total $24.93B; ratios: CET1 10.3%, Tier 1 11.1%, Total 12.8%, leverage 9.9%.
  - 2022—AENB: CET1/Tier 1 $14.82B; Total $17.27B; ratios: CET1 11.3%, Tier 1 11.3%, Total 13.2%, leverage 9.7%.
  - 2021—Company: CET1 $17.55B; Tier 1 $19.19B; Total $21.51B; ratios: CET1 10.5%, Tier 1 11.5%, Total 12.9%, leverage 10.5%.
  - 2021—AENB: CET1/Tier 1 $13.09B; Total $15.28B; ratios: CET1 11.8%, Tier 1 11.8%, Total 13.7%, leverage 10.5%.
- Regulatory thresholds:
  - Well-capitalized: Company—Tier 1 6%, Total 10% (no CET1 or leverage requirement for BHCs); AENB—CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8%, Total 10%, leverage 5%.
  - Minimums: CET1 4.5%, Tier 1 6%, Total 8%, leverage 4%.
  - Effective minimums (with buffers): CET1 7%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5%, leverage 4%; buffers include the stress capital buffer for the Company and the capital conservation buffer for AENB.
- Methodology and references: Ratios use Basel III capital definitions and the standardized approach; well-capitalized definitions per Federal Reserve Regulation Y and FDICIA.
- Restricted net assets: Certain subsidiaries face restrictions on transferring net assets due to debt and regulatory requirements; no impact on dividend policy to date and none anticipated; approximately $12.0B of subsidiary net assets were restricted as of December 31, 2022.

nodes.title: REGULATORY MATTERS AND CAPITAL ADEQUACY - Introduction
nodes.source_heading: NOTE 22 REGULATORY MATTERS AND CAPITAL ADEQUACY
nodes.heading: NOTE 22 REGULATORY MATTERS AND CAPITAL ADEQUACY
nodes.start_phrase: We are supervised and regulated by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (the Federal Reserve) and are subject to the Federal Reserve’s requirements for risk-based capital and leverage ratios.
nodes.summary: Overview of American Express Company’s and American Express National Bank’s (AENB) regulatory capital and leverage requirements under Federal Reserve and OCC supervision, using Basel III standardized approach. The section notes mandatory/discretionary regulatory actions if minimums are not met and confirms both entities met all requirements and exceeded “well capitalized” thresholds as of December 31, 2022 and 2021. It presents a table of CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, and Tier 1 leverage ratios and dollar capital amounts for both periods, including 2022 ratios: American Express Company CET1 10.3%, Tier 1 11.1%, Total 12.8%, leverage 9.9%; AENB CET1 11.3%, Tier 1 11.3%, Total 13.2%, leverage 9.7%. It also lists benchmark thresholds: minimums (4.5%/6.0%/8.0% capital; 4.0% leverage), “well capitalized” (for banks: 6.5%/8.0%/10.0%/5.0%; no CET1 or leverage for BHCs), and effective minimums including buffers (CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5%, leverage 4.0%), with buffers comprised of the stress capital buffer (company) and capital conservation buffer (bank), and references definitions under Regulation Y and FDICIA.

nodes.title: RESTRICTED NET ASSETS OF SUBSIDIARIES
nodes.heading: 22.1 RESTRICTED NET ASSETS OF SUBSIDIARIES
nodes.start_phrase: Certain of our subsidiaries are subject to restrictions on the transfer of net assets under debt agreements and regulatory requirements.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Note 22 summarizes American Express Company’s regulatory oversight, capital adequacy framework, capital ratios, restrictions on subsidiary net asset transfers, and dividend limitations for both the holding company and its bank subsidiary, American Express National Bank (AENB).

- Regulatory framework:
  - The Company is supervised by the Federal Reserve; AENB is supervised by the OCC.
  - Subject to Basel III risk-based capital (CET1, Tier 1, Total) and Tier 1 leverage requirements under the standardized approach.
  - Failure to meet minimums can trigger mandatory and discretionary regulatory actions.

- Compliance status and capital ratios:
  - As of December 31, 2022 and 2021, both the Company and AENB met all capital requirements and exceeded “well-capitalized” thresholds.
  - 2022 ratios:
    - American Express Company: CET1 10.3%, Tier 1 11.1%, Total 12.8%, Tier 1 leverage 9.9%.
    - AENB: CET1 11.3%, Tier 1 11.3%, Total 13.2%, Tier 1 leverage 9.7%.
  - 2021 ratios:
    - American Express Company: CET1 10.5%, Tier 1 11.5%, Total 12.9%, Tier 1 leverage 10.5%.
    - AENB: CET1 11.8%, Tier 1 11.8%, Total 13.7%, Tier 1 leverage 10.5%.

- Regulatory thresholds and buffers:
  - Minimum capital ratios: CET1 4.5%, Tier 1 6.0%, Total 8.0%, leverage 4.0%.
  - “Well-capitalized” (for banks): CET1 6.5%, Tier 1 8.0%, Total 10.0%, leverage 5.0%.
  - Effective minimums including buffers: CET1 7.0%, Tier 1 8.5%, Total 10.5%, leverage 4.0% (stress capital buffer for the holding company; capital conservation buffer for AENB).

- Restricted net assets of subsidiaries:
  - About $12.0 billion of subsidiary net assets were restricted from transfer at December 31, 2022.
  - These restrictions have not affected, and are not expected to affect, shareholder dividend policy; processes exist to transfer assets in compliance with constraints.

- Dividend restrictions:
  - Bank holding company (American Express Company): Dividends are subject to Federal Reserve policies—generally limited to net income of the past year and must align with capital needs, asset quality, and financial condition. The Company must be a source of strength to its bank and maintain an annual capital plan; dividends may be limited if capital ratios fall below requirements/buffers or if capital plans must be resubmitted.
  - Bank subsidiary (AENB): Paid $4.6 billion in dividends to the parent in 2022. Dividends are limited to retained earnings and cannot jeopardize capital standards; if capital ratios and buffers are not met, dividends and other distributions face graduated constraints. Regulators can restrict dividends deemed unsafe or unsound.

nodes.title: BANK HOLDING COMPANY DIVIDEND RESTRICTIONS
nodes.heading: 22.2 BANK HOLDING COMPANY DIVIDEND RESTRICTIONS
nodes.start_phrase: We are limited in our ability to pay dividends by the Federal Reserve, which could prohibit a dividend that would be considered an unsafe or unsound banking practice.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of restrictions on dividends for a bank holding company and its bank subsidiary, emphasizing regulatory limits tied to safety and soundness.
- Federal Reserve policy for bank holding companies: dividends should be paid only from net income available to common shareholders generated over the past year and align with capital needs, asset quality, and financial condition.
- “Source of strength” doctrine: holding companies must support insured depository subsidiaries and avoid dividend practices that weaken this ability.
- Requirement to maintain an annual capital plan that includes planned dividends; potential limitations if regulatory capital ratios fall short of minimums/buffers or if the capital plan must be resubmitted.
- Bank-level restrictions (AENB example): in 2022, AENB paid $4.6 billion in dividends to its parent from retained earnings.
- Banking laws and regulations generally prohibit dividends without approval if not from available retained earnings or if distributions would breach capital adequacy standards.
- If risk-based capital ratios and buffers are not met, AENB faces graduated constraints on dividends and other capital distributions.
- Dividend determinations must consider risk-based capital and leverage ratio requirements and relevant regulatory policy statements.
- Banking regulators can limit or prohibit bank dividends if deemed unsafe or unsound given the institution’s financial condition.

nodes.title: BANK DIVIDEND RESTRICTIONS
nodes.heading: 22.3 BANK DIVIDEND RESTRICTIONS
nodes.start_phrase: In the year ended December 31, 2022, AENB paid dividends from retained earnings to its parent of $4.6 billion.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Federal Reserve constraints on dividends by bank holding companies: dividends should be paid only from net income available to common shareholders over the prior year, subject to prospective capital needs, asset quality, and overall condition; parent companies must serve as a source of strength to bank subsidiaries; dividends are incorporated into an annual capital plan and may be limited if regulatory capital ratios fall below minimums/buffers or if a capital plan must be resubmitted.
- Details bank-level dividend restrictions for American Express National Bank (AENB): paid $4.6 billion of dividends to its parent in 2022 from retained earnings; dividends generally must come from retained earnings and cannot compromise capital adequacy; if risk-based capital ratios and buffers are not met, dividends and other capital distributions face graduated constraints; regulators can limit or prohibit dividends deemed unsafe or unsound.
- Presents Note 23 on significant credit concentrations: maximum on-balance sheet credit exposure totaled $213 billion at December 31, 2022 (vs. $172 billion in 2021).
- Breaks down 2022 exposure: Individuals $156B (United States $129B; outside the U.S. $27B); Institutions—financial services $36B, other institutions $17B; U.S. Government and agencies $4B.
- Explains risk management governance: consumer and small business exposures managed under individual credit risk; corporate exposures under institutional credit risk; bank/broker/insurer exposures under institutional credit risk; government exposures managed by the Asset and Liability Management Committee; major non-U.S. concentrations include the U.K., Japan, EU, Australia, Canada, and Mexico.
- Notes the largest concentration is unsecured credit to individuals; underwriting includes application review, assessment of financial history, and evaluation of ability/willingness to repay; performance is monitored by tenure, industry, and geography.
- Discloses unused credit of approximately $350B in 2022 (vs. $327B in 2021), about 80% in the U.S.; unused amounts may not be drawn; charge card products without pre-set spending limits are excluded from unused credit.

nodes.title: SIGNIFICANT CREDIT CONCENTRATIONS
nodes.heading: NOTE 23 SIGNIFICANT CREDIT CONCENTRATIONS
nodes.start_phrase: Concentrations of credit risk exist when changes in economic, industry or geographic factors similarly affect groups of counterparties whose aggregate credit exposure is material in relation to American Express’ total credit exposure.
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on American Express’ credit risk concentrations and segment reporting.
- Note 23 (Significant Credit Concentrations):
  - Explains concentration risk and that customers span diverse industries and regions.
  - Presents maximum on-balance sheet credit exposure as of Dec 31:
    - Total: $213B (2022) vs $172B (2021).
    - Individuals: $156B (2022) vs $131B (2021), primarily consumer and small business loans/receivables under individual credit risk management.
    - Geography: U.S. $129B vs $108B; Outside U.S. $27B vs $23B (noting largest regions include the U.K., Japan, EU, Australia, Canada, Mexico).
    - Institutions: Financial services $36B vs $24B; Other institutions $17B vs $15B (governed by institutional credit risk management).
    - U.S. Government and agencies: $4B vs $2B (managed by Asset and Liability Management Committee).
  - Identifies individuals as the most significant credit concentration; exposures largely unsecured but mitigated through underwriting (financial history, capacity/willingness to repay) and monitoring by tenure, industry, and geography.
  - Notes approximately $350B (2022) and $327B (2021) of unused credit, ~80% U.S.; much is not expected to be drawn. Charge cards have no preset spending limit and are excluded from unused credit.
- Note 24 (Reportable Operating Segments and Geographic Operations):
  - Describes factors used to define segments (CODM review, economics, products/services, customer classes, distribution, geography, regulation).
  - Notes 2022 changes: updated revenue allocation methodology (Q1 2022) and segment realignment (Q3 2022), with prior periods recast.
  - Defines four reportable segments:
